listRow.content: Regarded as the backyard of Paris, the Jardin du Luxembourg attracts an endless stream of Parisians and international tourists alike. Its flower beds are the most eye-catching areas of the park; offering a visual feast throughout the year with carefully curated seasonal colors determined by the floral varieties and designs. Hung Jui-Lin visited Paris on his tour of Europe in 1980. He uses highly saturated colors to punctuate the flowerbeds in front of which pedestrians pass, and tourists sit to chat and bask in the sun. Uninhibited in his brushstrokes, he depicts the figures in white, casting shadows in purple. The painting is dominated by purple and green hues. The purple shadows cast by the figures in the foreground echoes the steps and railings in the distance above the garden. Hung Jui-Lin uses pastels and oils interchangeably, with pastels as the base, and oils added to depict the structures and shapes of trees and buildings within the garden. There are several swirls of pastel clouds in the sky, conveying the artist’s joyous and unconventional mood while creating this work. Hung Jui-Lin preserves the romance and vibrancy of Paris in this lighthearted work. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

listRow.content: With her long hair cascading over her shoulders, this model is seated with her knees drawn in, with her face tilted toward the left as though in contemplation. Her chin is supported by her right hand, and her left hand is draped naturally on her left knee. Hung Jui-Lin has created the arc of her back, hips, and legs in a single brushstroke. A darker, thick arc line on her left hip, cushion, and left calf express shadowed areas. Flesh toned watercolor has been applied all over the form of the body to illustrate the softness of her flesh. In contrast, the unilluminated areas of her right hand, chest, left hand, right thigh and calf are shaded using a similar hue that is differentiated through layering. It is difficult to create depth in the nude by using water colors to create a complex form with minimal differences in color. Interest is created by expressing difference in light and shading through color, and the occasional overlapping or mutual rendering of color, as evident between her face and neck, her right arm and chest, or her hair and right arm. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 28

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin’s Academy of Arts student, Hwang Yuan-Ching, once said in an interview, “After he arranges the model’s pose, Professor Hung would take advantage of his free time to make many quick studies. He mostly used bamboo brush and ink wash to paint, amalgamating Eastern and Western methods of expression. He shows his students how quick studies can be expressed from many perspectives and can be integrated with Eastern art.” This work attests to Hung Jui-Lin’s typical technique for painting female nudes and the concepts he expresses. This model’s hands are raised and resting on her head, standing tall with her chest out. The rounded, slender curves of her body from her back, waist and hips to her thighs and feet are the type of elegant posture specific to women. The light source in the painting comes from behind the model, hence her chest, lower abdomen, and inner right calf are in shadow. Using the rendering of a wet brush, Hung Jui-Lin creates a chiaroscuro in her form, providing an unequivocal example for his students. Through the years, the subject of Hung Jui-Lin’s nudes has consistently been the female form, but he persistently challenges himself with the myriad of poses.  (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

listRow.content:
Hung Jui-Lin’s son Chin S. Houng operated a number of restaurants in the Redondo Beach area of Los Angeles. In 1980, Hung Jui-Lin officially immigrated to the United States. This small work in pastel was presumably completed in 1979 when Hung Jui-Lin visited his son. He painted the Palos Verdes Peninsula south of Redondo Beach. There are many homes on the mountains of Palos Verdes, and he enjoyed the beaches at Torrance, the everchanging colorful clouds at sunset, which he developed into the “Sun, Cloud, Sea” series. 

In this work, there are layers of blue and green on the sea’s surface. The sky is of intertwined lavender, blue, and pale yellow clouds that express a romantic and elegant atmosphere. Tourists on the beach strolled along or chatted. This was very different from his life in Taiwan, and a thematic and stylistic transformation began to take shape in the artist. Hung Jui-Lin said, “The coastal areas of the United States change with the weather. They are beautiful scenic areas. One could say that the weather is great every day, and emotionally I also followed the sunshine.”  (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Redondo Beach, Los Angeles County

listRow.content:
This 1979 painting depicts the landscape of a residential area of Los Angeles in the U.S. Hung Jui-Lin’s oldest son, Chin S. Houng, lived in the Torrance area of Los Angeles in the U.S. Established over a century ago, Old Town Torrance is notable for its Spanish hacienda-style architecture with terracotta-tiled rooves, whitewalls, arches and long corridors. Hung Jui-Lin had visited this district numerous times prior to painting this work, gradually becoming familiar with the streets and houses in the area.

The sunlight, architecture, and vegetation of Los Angeles was different from that of his home in Taiwan, and stimulated his creative inspiration. He uses pencil to sketch the gentle hills in the distance dotted with villas and houses. The vista of high-rises and residential areas from a bird’s-eye-view was likely painted from a position high above in order to access such an expansive panorama. The pencil sketch is attentive to creating chiaroscuro. Though no color is applied, the work has a high degree of completion. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

listRow.content: This sketchbook on the theme of female nudes was started in March 1978, and includes 25 works of female nudes, 10 of which are in ink wash, nine in pencil, and six in ballpoint pen – media that is easily within hand’s reach. The models are in a variety of poses include standing, seated, reclined. Hung Jui-Lin would guide models to pose for the students to sketch. Hung Jui-Lin’s female nudes number in the thousands, and are an important artistic expression for him following his quick sketches of miners. These nudes in thousands of different poses were each completed by Hung Jui-Lin within a few minutes or less. It provides an understanding into his grasp of the human form. His nudes notably convey elegance and atmosphere, as well as brush and ink interest. In February of that year, Hung Jui-Lin’s wife Peng Jin-Hua passed away, and he was striving to adapt to a new way of life. Teaching allowed him to interact with students, and painting provided some consolation from the devastation of losing his wife. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Sketchbook 7

listRow.content: Under Hung Jui-Lin’s brush, the female nude often expresses the elegant subtle beauty of the Eastern woman. This particular model is distinct in her stance with her left arm akimbo, her right palm extended downward in a forward direction and her left foot raised and stepping forward, with her weight on her right leg. There is a dynamism in this action that id different from a static posture. Hung Jui-Lin’s angle of depiction is from the back and side of the model. Her upright form is reminiscent of a dance pose. The strong muscles in her hips and legs leaves the viewer with a strong visual impression. Diluted ink has been applied over the model’s entire body, with liubai (leaving blank) on the edges of her left breast, her right arm, her curved left arm and left thigh, and her left and right foot, enabling the viewer to see that the light is coming from the front and side of the model. The model’s head and the hair on her left side has been scraped white by the paint brush. A few blue lines have been added to increase the degree of darkness on her hips, breast, right arm, inner thigh, and the back of her calves. The artist has carefully cleaned up details in the painting. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 26

listRow.content: The female nude in the painting seems at ease and relaxed as she exposes her body. She is in a semi-reclined position, with her left arm propped up straight on the pedestal and her five fingers outstretched as though there is some strain on the left hand. Her left calf is crossed at her right calf, with her right foot on tiptoes. The light source illuminates the model from the right, hence, from her right cheek to the right side of her chest, her left shoulder, the right side of her waist and her right thigh, and left inner thigh have been left blank to express brightness; while diluted ink has been applied to the opposite side. On the model’s right hairline and chin, Hung Jui-Lin has added a few strokes with a blue marker as through correcting the lines of the chin and emphasizing the darkness of the hair. Hung Jui-Lin said, “The Chinese body is beautiful. Where does this beauty lie? Foreigners are pretty on the surface, but our beauty is within. We are reserved and reticent about open expression; ours is an internal beauty.” The internal beauty Hung Jui-Lin refers to is the beauty of subtlety. The internal beauty of the Eastern woman can be seen here, as well as her veauty of confidence. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 25

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin says, “My female nudes differ from Western versions. The lines vary in their intensity and degree of suppleness, and embody emotion.” This model is semi-reclined in a pose that is traditionally seen in sketches of nudes Hung Jui-Lin’s carefree and undeliberate lines thoroughly capture the posture of the female nude. The figure’s center of gravity is distributed between her lower body and her right wrist. Thick, broad lines have been applied to the dense curly shoulder length hair, arms, and chest, using the thick black lines to indicate shadows. The same technique has been used where the right calf meets the fabric cushion and the contour lines above the left calf. Large swaths of light are seen above the model’s chest, her lower abdomen, and her thighs; areas in shadow have been depicted by applying a wet brush of diluted ink, or by rubbing with a dry brush and leaving leaving areas of flying-white (kasuri) at the points of pivot. Unconcerned with the diluted ink spilling over the contour lines, his expression of light and shadows are unique. Hung Jui-Lin completes the nudes in the classroom as a demonstration for the students as well as to elevate his own powers of expression. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 24

listRow.content: The female nudes under Hung Jui-Lin’s brush often break from the traditional poses to recreate the internal strength and personality of the modern woman beyond gentility and grace. This work that features a model in a kneeling position sketched from behind is rarely seen, and conveys a sense of youth and playfulness. According to Lai Wu Hsiung who studied under Hung Jui-Lin at the Academy of Arts, “Professor Hung’s sketching class was relaxed. On the day, he discussed the pose and atmosphere to be considered with the model. After an explanation and discussion, he begins sketching along with the students.” The model’s unctuously-inked voluminous ponytail carries weight. The contours of her back and upturned buttocks and well-proportioned thighs are precisely expressed in a single line. This work completes the human form with minimal brushwork. Diluted ink has been brushed lightly like water over the body, with the ink rendering forming blended to form a sketch with a sense of volume as well as the softness of the female form. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 23

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin expresses his pursuit of authenticity and beauty through his creative endeavors. Authenticity was found in painting the true temperament of the miners; and on his pursuit of beauty, he said, “The part of my life that is ‘beauty’ are the female nudes. Beauty is my point of departure in this pursuit, which is different from the intensive life of struggle among miners. The two points are disparate in their essence.” The beauty of female nudes are in the soft lines that represent the supple aesthetic of the human body. It is a carefree satisfaction as well as an expression of the artist’s whimsy. With her fingers interlaced, the model in this painting hugs her left leg in a seated position. The elevated left leg and the naturally draped right leg are the focal point in this pose, as well as the most challenging aspect of dimensionality to express. With her body leaning slightly toward the back, the model has squared shoulders that offset the voluptuous fullness of her hips and thighs in the foreground. The unilluminated areas such as her hair, face, chest, waist, and inner right thigh have been shaded using rendered diluted ink. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

listRow.content: This double-sided painting includes sketches of the same model from two opposite angles. The well-proportioned model is in an attractive pose with thighs together and her calves apart. She is seated on a fabric-covered round stool. Her right hand lightly rests on her knee, and her left hand is raised behind her neck, as though arranging her hair in a pose that exudes feminine elegance. The artist has first outlined the contours of the model’s form using a fine bamboo brush, and then retraced the lines using various diluted colors for emphasis. For instance, her chest in a maroon color, and the thighs in brown. The model’s body is painted using diluted colors, with the light and shading expressed using careful rendering. The light source is to the left of the model, which the artist has expressed using a light flesh tone on her hair, left shoulder, waist, left thigh, and left calf; the brightest point is on the white fabric covering the footstool. The right side of the body is unilluminated, and the faint cyan and green applied on top of the flesh tones mixes with diluted ink to create an elegant hue. Behind the model and along the contours of the human form, the same cyan and green hues dissolve into diluted ink to create a background that off sets the high chroma and brightness of the model. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 21

listRow.content:
This work likely depicts the same model featured in Quick Sketch, Female Nude 19 from a different angle. Her head is tilted slightly to the right, and her center of gravity leans toward the right of the painting. Her left arm blocks the peripheral contours of her thigh and hip closest to the viewer. She is propped up by her left arm, with her thighs folded together over her calves. Her right calf and the sole of her right foot can be seen. The right hand has been concealed from this angle, a pose that is difficult to depict. The artist’s observes as he wields his brush, which can be discerned from the hesitations in his brushstrokes. The placement and lifting of the thickly inked brush creates areas of flying white (kasuri), the varying thickness of the confident lines are full of interest. 

Ink rubbed by a dry brush create the tussled strands of the figure’s hair, with areas of liubai (leaving blank) indicating areas of shine. Her face is tilted downward, with her eyes closed as though in thought. There are no renderings of diluted ink on her torso, but a sense of undulating flesh is conveyed, with a single arced line expressing a sense of weight in her chest, lower abdomen, and thighs. Hung Jui-Lin uses brushstrokes similar to caoshu calligraphy in this female nude. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 20

listRow.content: Using traditional Chinese brush and ink on rice paper to paint female nudes, Hung Jui-Lin accurately grasps the human form using simple lines, and quickly expresses lights and shadows. Head bowed, the model in the painting is seated on a fabric covered cushion with her left arm propped up on the undulating cushion, with her hip and legs resting on the cloth cushion. The model’s body has been outlined using a thick saturated inked brush. The model is illuminated mainly from a light source that seems to be positioned close in front of her, as though sitting up in bed, facing the light. The model’s shadow is projected onto the wall, along with the shadows cast by students sketching. This background depiction is rare among his female nudes. The work goes beyond the customary nature of human character sketches. Rendered by moisture, the scene of students sketching at the easels has a realistic yet blurred presentation. Hung Jui-Lin faithfully depicts the enlarged shadow of the female nude subject, and creates artistry from the scene before him using ink. The use of brush and ink on rice paper enables with ease the expression of a scene created by light in a short period of time. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin taken a perspective above the horizon line to depict this model with her left hand in her hair, and her right hand on her hip. Due to this perspective, the figure’s legs seem particularly short and her buttocks appear full. Full buttocks are commonly seen in the body shape of Eastern women. This work depicts the nude from the back. The proportions of her body highlight her voluptuous buttocks and thighs, while her left arm resting on her head seem short. The artist is concise in his brush work without repeating brushstrokes. The rendering of wet ink on cotton paper underscores the sense of dimensionality. Areas of chiaroscuro are indicated in the contour lines of the human body and the liubai (leaving blank) spaces. Lithe, curving lines in the shoulder blades, spine, and hips highlight the three-dimensionality of the human body. Using dots of warm, moist diluted ink, Hung Jui-Lin renders the contours in the textures of flesh and bones. The seemingly casual brush stroke where the spine meets the buttocks conveys his understanding of the musculature and anatomy in his ease of depiction. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 18

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin uses the same media in his female nudes and miner paintings, which is most often brush and ink. He believes that the bamboo brush is better able to express his intentions, with more control over the variations in the strength of lines. The figure in this work may be the same model as the figure in Quick Sketch, Female Nude 18, though one is a back view and the other has been painted in profile. From the ink rendering on the contours, it is clear that the artist has used a continuous line from the moment the wet brush touches paper until it ran dry before he lifts the brush. The model gazes toward her right, with her left arm akimbo and legs slightly apart. Her face is obscured by hair of texturized ink. Uneven diluted ink has been rendered with a large brush on her left arm, left torso, left thigh, and inner right thigh. Illuminated areas are depicted as liubai (leaving blank), and the darkest area is the hair. Due to the absorbency of the paper, wet diluted ink is spread across the body, leaving rendered watermarks where ink was applied. Hong Jui-Lin continuously experimented with the simple theme of the female nude using a variety of media, revealing the artist’s prolific creative prowess. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 17

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin advocated painting the human body as a starting point for those learning to paint, because everyone is familiar with the human body. As a subject for learning and creativity, the human body is rich in its balance, mutability, dynamism, and rhythm When students delve into sketching the human form, they must establish the correct concepts, and lay the foundations for sketching through practice, hence, he often encourages students to not only begin with sketching female nudes but also to continuously improve themselves. In this work, the model has taken a seated pose with both arms raised above her head as though arrange her hair into a bun. Her thighs overlap and there is a circular sense overall. The model’s eyes are peacefully closed and without expression. The artist has created a continuous line of varying thickness from her right waist to her right thigh. This was drawn in a continuous stroke. Where the right leg meets the left has also been depicted in one continuous line, then retraced. The edges of the right arm and right thigh have been darkened with a thick brush to indicate shadows. No colors were applied to this work which expresses the volume and illumination of the human form with pure lines. It is a simple, frank, and unpretentious expression of the image of the female nude. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 16

title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 15
medium: Ink, pigment, and pastel on cotton paper

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin said in 1990, “The works depicting female nudes contrasts with that of the miners. I used my spare time between teaching at the Academy of Arts to paint a little. It reminded me of the foundations of painting that I studied while in Japan. The way I felt at the time gave me freedom in my methods of expression.” This nude was painted by the sexagenarian Hung Jui-Lin. Recalling his own attitude of rigorous learning while in Japan, he especially reveled in his access to the joy of creativity. By guiding the models in their poses, he enabled students to not only grasp techniques in sketching the human form, but also experience the joy of live sketching. The left arm of this model wraps around the back of her waist, with her left hand resting on the right arm that is pressed against her hip. Her left leg is flexed and her right leg is straightened. A diluted light gray has been applied over this human form, with highlights at the nose, right shoulder, and chest, through the slender waist onto the hip. The shaded areas include the left of the neck, left, shoulder, left chest. The brushwork in the outline of the human contours are harmonious and precise in this sketch, with nimble shifts in the thickness of the lines. The transitions, pauses, or repeated strokes for emphasis are very natural. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

listRow.content: The female nude is a classic theme in Western art, as well as a symbol in praise of beauty. Using Eastern ink wash with the bamboo brush as a medium combined with Western pastels, Hung Jui-Lin expresses the Western painting tradition though a methodology that integrates Eastern and Western painting traditions in his unique style. This can be attributed to following in his father’s calligraphy and plum paintings since childhood. Over the course the next 50 to 60 years, he mastered the Eastern media of ink wash and paper, and accumulated precious artistic achievements through his ceaseless sketches of mine workers. This female nude takes a standing pose, with her head tilted toward her extended right arm, only half of which is depicted. Her left hand is held close to her body, with her left leg slightly bent back. This intentionally posed stance is full of dynamism, as though a crystalized moment of dance. The left half of the body is in the shade, which Hung Jui-Lin has expressed through an agile application of rendered ink. Yellow pastel has been applied to the arm, chest and waist on the right, adding to the sense of light. The elegant demeanor of the subject suggests a dancer’s aesthetic, and a feminine beauty as expressed by the artist. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 13

listRow.content:
Hung Jui-Lin has said, “I am also a straightforward person, and not one who lives through the mind or rationale. My paintings emphasize the emotions. If I want to paint something, I would naturally paint it.” The emotions behind painting a female nude is different from that of painting miners. Painting miners is dynamic, with a degree of tension and intensity. Female nudes are a more tranquil pursuit, approached with a calmer heart. This is a drastic contrast. Perfectly Illustrative Hung Jui-Lin’s explanation, the posture of this female nude is graceful with a subtle expression.

In this painting, the model’s tilts her head shyly. She is propped up by outstretched arms with her hands on the platform on which she is seated, although the platform itself is not depicted. Her body is voluptuous and full, with the beauty of the human form fully expressed under Hung Jui-Lin’s brush. Thicker, more saturated lines express the unilluminated areas of the chest, arms, waist and left calf. Yellow pastel color express the areas of illumination on the right cheek, right shoulder, chest, and two thighs. Where paintings of miners express male masculinity, female nudes are rich in the beauty of the gentle, rounded body which Hung Jui-Lin vividly interprets. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 12

listRow.content: A return to the theme of female nudes developed when he was teaching at the Academy of Arts, and began sketching nude models with his students. His dedication to sketching the human form during his studies in Japan, and his 35 years devoted to capturing the dynamism of the miners at the colliery had brought his skills to an expert level. By his 60s in 1975, artistic creation was one of his life’s great pleasures. In this work, the model is facing forward, with her body at an angle and sitting elegantly with her legs crossed. The consistent thickness of the brushstrokes outlines the human form. Areas unexposed to directly light such as the face, chest, lower abdomen, and left inner thigh have been with a light reddish brown pastel, while illuminated areas such as the right cheek, right shoulder, right waist, right thigh, and the left inner calf have been highlighted with yellow pastel color, while the right arm has been emphasized using light orange lines. The woman’s head is proportionally smaller than her elongated body. This slender woman’s posture is natural and self-assured, expressing a feminine beauty. The artist’s unhurried and relaxed state of mind is also reflected I n the work. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 11
medium: Ink, pigment, and pastel on cotton paper

listRow.content: Female nudes form a complement to Hung Jui-Lin’s years of focus on the theme of miners. Miners express the ruggedness of the human body and the power in lines; while female nudes express the elegance and adroitness of lines. This work has been painted on light green cotton paper, and presents the elegant beauty of the female nude through flowing lines. The model’s arms are lifted up with her hands crossing behind her head. She sits in profile with both legs dangling and her toes touching lightly on the ground, which forms an upward elongated effect in the painting, making her body appear more slender. Yellow pastel color has been applied to the brightest areas, creating a golden light on the body that recalls the glow of sunset. The shaded areas in the figure’s back and buttocks have been emphasized with rendered flesh-toned watercolors to increase the sense of dimensionality. The arcs of the body’s curves create a rhythmic lightness. Her hands are clasped behind her head, seemingly preoccupied with thought. Upon his retirement, Hung Jui-Lin welcomed a relaxed and carefree realm of life, which catalyzed innovative methods for the artist that differed from those of the past.  and also began creative methodology that differed from his past. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 11

tfam.Media Technology: Ink, pigment, and pastel on cotton paper

listRow.content: This nude in a sitting fetal position reveals the elegant curves of the back and buttocks. Hung Jui-Lin has outlined the silhouette of her body simply using a single black line. Besides the saturated black on her hair, diluted ink has replaced outline in tracing the silhouette of her back and buttocks, through her thigh, and in depicting the spine at the center of her back and the ribs across her right side. Her bone structure and musculature have also been created with brushes of diluted ink. The darkest areas are in the curves of her armpits and the bend of her thigh, where her hips meet the thighs, and her thick, dark hair. Hung Jui-Lin has outlined these areas with a wet brush with saturated ink. The rendering effect of the lines express shading. This type of contrast painting technique is rarely seen. The cloth draped on the seat cushion has been cleverly expressed using random ink brush lines. When facing a live model, Hung Jui-Lin would alter his technique at will, adjusting his media and method of expression according to the conditions in the moment. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 10

title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 9
medium: Ink, pigment, and pastel on cotton paper

listRow.content: This work is among very few sketches by the artist that include the model’s facial expression. Here, Hung Jui-Lin uses the simple lines of a dry brush on colored paper. Rendered diluted ink creates the changes in light and shadow, and the undulating musculature on the model’s body. A single stroke confidently outlines everything from her face to her shoulders, left arm, breasts, and legs. A touch of yellow and light green pastel color have been applied on her nose, chest, abdomen, and illuminated upper thigh as the liubai (leaving blank) on the paper is not sufficient in depicting the areas of light. The diluted ink behind the body creates a depth of space. The graceful expression of the model’s face and her elegant sitting posture imbues the work with a sense of serenity. According to Hung Jui-Lin, his sketches of the female nude must express the gentle beauty of femininity. Through his brushwork and painting style, he does indeed reveal the idea of inner beauty. Hung Jui-Lin believes “Art would be lacklustre without the presence of feminine beauty.” (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

listRow.content: After retiring from the colliery in 1972, Hung Jui-Lin’s lifestyle changed, and the themes of his paintings changed as well. In his free time, he often went outdoors with his students and other painters in pursuit of sunshine, to reclaim the joys of painting en plein air. The tools for watercolor paintings were light and easy to carry, so he had a proclivity for sketching with watercolors. The Taiwanese landscape paintings in watercolor during this era were obviously lighter and brighter than the works depicting mine workers. This painting depicting a traditional sihe courtyard home was a sketch made in Pingtung in 1973. This is southern Fujian style of architecture familiar to him in his youth. The classic elements of the traditional houses: horseback roof ridge and gable walls, the redbrick exterior wall with green balustrade, are the focus of his expression. Using scenes of Taiwanese country homes as his subject, Hung Jui-Lin reveals his nostalgia and sentimentality for his homeland. Hung Jui-Lin’s painting of the rustic country village, with his steadfast brush work, clear color palate, and stable perspective, are unexaggerated and reveal his character of candor and sincerity. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

listRow.content: After the model settles into her pose, Hung Jui-Lin would observe from various angles and select an angle he believes to be most beautiful from which to sketch. Leaning against a vertical cabinet, this model has her hair to one side, her fingers are relaxed, her left arm is draped behind her. The sketch seems to be slightly deformed and out of proportion at first glance, but the work is an example of the artist’s own ideals and techniques applied in the process of depicting a live subject to create a work of interest. The right leg and foot of this female nude was first sketched using a fine tipped brush, and then immediately brushed over with a wet brush of diluted ink, dissolving the line in the diluted ink. The left leg and left foot have been similarly outlined with a fine point brush, but the ink is darker and relatively dry and maintains vivid after the wash of diluted ink. The two legs create a perceptual contrast. The variations in line thickness creates a shift. The diluted ink follows the posture of the upper body leaning against the cabinet to create directionality and shadows. The work is tactile and painterly. The artist did not portray the model faithfully, but followed his instincts to create a unique work. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

listRow.content: Completed in April 1971, Hung Jui-Lin produced this sketchbook on the invitation of Ni Hou-Tai, the eldest son of Mr. Ni Chiang-Huai, when he worked as mine manager at the Daxi Coalmine owned by Ni and his partners. The sketchbook includes 34 works from the Daxi Coalmine period. Hung Jui-Lin’s eldest daughter Hung Bai-Yun has labeled the cover with August 24, 1991. Other than six works depicting dogs, the remainder of the works are sketches of mineworkers; including one individual portrait, and several portraits of groups of two or three miners. The majority are scenes featuring crowds of miners. They are discussing issues encountered within the mine pit, or work progress; there are also scenes of gatherings, waiting, or resting outside the mine. There are no depictions of work inside the pit, which indicates that at age 60, Hung Jui-Lin no longer entered the pit to make sketches. These quick sketches of mine workers were completed using pencil, bamboo brush, and diluted colors. Among these is a pencil sketch of miners gathered in discussion at the adit to the mine pit which Hung Jui-Lin had hoped to convert into an oil painting, but was unable to complete. This was his final oil work depicting mine workers. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

listRow.content: This work was completed on July 2, 1971. It is the last of the five self-portraits that have been preserved. Completed in 1932, the earliest self-portrait was donated to the Museum in 1987. The facial features in this work have been drawn using a blue fine point marker, the contours of the hair and shirt, and the shadowed regions of the chin and under the collar, as well as the dark eyebrows, hair, and lips, have been conveyed through saturated blocks constituted of dense lines. Perhaps the effect was not as intended, so the addition of saturated and light pigmentation and intentional blank spaces (liubai) have been utilized to express light and shadow. The light in the painting comes from the right; hence, his right cheek is not illuminated. A rendering of light pigmentation has been applied to suggest the shadowed side with a vertical line to indicate slenderness. The illuminated left side of the nose and cheek have been left blank (liubai). Hung Jui-Lin created several self-portraits between 1932 and 1971, each capturing the artist’s state of mind in that moment. At the time this self-portrait was created, Hung was still employed at the Daxi Coalmine. The work was subsequently published in Lion Art Magazine in 1979. Hung retired from the mines in 1972, and from that point forward, no longer depicted mine workers in his works. He emerged from the darkness into light, pivoting to en plein air landscapes and female nudes as his main subjects. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

title: The Mona Lisa in the Mirror

listRow.Title: The Mona Lisa in the Mirror

listRow.content: The pose this model takes, seated with her head bowed reading a book in her hand, is quite elegant; it is also a pose that can be sustained for a relatively long period. There is a sculptural sense to this pose, which is often used for sketching in academic settings. Using his observation, Hung Jui-Lin eschews the brush and ink expressions of line thickness, ink intensity, and rendering, and sketches this nude using a permanent marker. Sketching directly from observation without a rough draft, the rigid tip of the marker does not allow for the completion of an extended line on a single stroke. Hence, there are areas of hesitation and pivoting in the powerful lines of the silhouette, though they connect to create a sense of voluptuous feminine volume while maintaining the suppleness of the musculature. The brushstrokes are precise in expressing the shadows, creating a three-dimensionality to the human body. Hung Jui-Lin uses various media in his expressions on the theme of the female nude, providing students in this foundational course at the academy with an excellent demonstration and inspiration. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 7

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin frankly stated that, “Drawing with ink wash better expresses the strength and the thickness and thinness of my lines. It is better suited to my intentions in my drawings.” This quick sketch of the human body is quite carefree. Two strokes depict the pectoral muscles, a circle represents the abdomen, the facial features are abstract and indistinguishable – which indicates the speed with which this was completed, almost without thought. There is a border of rendered ink and dry brush on the periphery of the portrait. The model is bowed in silence. The depiction of this figure reveals a sculptural tendency with a sense of tenacious resilience and an inner strength in the rounded lines. For Hung Jui-Lin, this brushwork is inspired, and is an attempt at a style rarely seen. This simplified study of a human figure should inspire students to seek out other perspectives for quick studies. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Quick Sketch of Human Form

listRow.content: Traditionally, the model would sit on a pedestal or chair while the artist sketches. Hung Jui-Lin prefers that models change their posture so that his students can practice a variety of shapes and angles. In this female nude, the model is on her knees, leaning slightly forward. This pose cannot be sustained for long, and requires the artist to rapidly sketch without a rough draft. Her back, buttocks, thighs, and calves are sketched directly, revealing feminine arced lines. The lines on the left side of this silhouette are darker and more intense than on the right, especially around the waist and hips where the lines vividly express shadows. A dry brush was used on the right to drag out an outline, naturally creating a flying white (飛白) effect to reveal the illuminated surfaces. A diluted green and ink have been brushed over the areas in shadow, with the liubai (leaving white) technique used to depict illuminated surfaces. Her skin is smooth and translucent; and the outlines on her calf muscles and soles are confident. This female nude accomplished through seasoned brush techniques have no narrative purpose and are without intentional layout. His precision and painterly character can be clearly discerned. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 6

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin feels that in comparing female nudes of the East and West, the Western proportions of the Western nude are truly elegant, but the Eastern nude embodies a tacit beauty, an expression of inner beauty. Comparing the two, Hung Jui-Lin has an appreciation for the female nudes of the East. This female back nude presents the human form in a few simple strokes, A single brushstroke at the center of the back reveals the concave lines of the spine. The white space on the left shoulder, left thigh, and the back of the left hand subtly reveals areas of light. Watercolors in varying shades reveal the rise and fall of the musculature over the entire back and buttocks. The artist has emphasized the exterior lines of the model’s two arms using thick dark outlines which not only highlights the skin tone and body shape, but also creates a spatial distance that separates the model from the background. The artist’s delicate brushwork depicts the supple texture of the seat cushion. Simple and harmonious, color has been applied to the seat cushion and the background in the same hue. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 5

listRow.content: The sentiment behind painting a female nude is to convey “beauty.” In Hung Jui-Lin’s life, female nudes represent beauty, and beauty is his point of departure in his approach to working with female nudes. This seated female nude from the back in profile seems slightly off balance as the seat cushion has been omitted. With the light source behind her, her raven hair becomes a grey-blue where illuminated, and her back, buttocks, and the soles of her feet are highlighted in a soft yellow tint where the light strikes. Her face, breasts, right thigh, and left calf are shielded from the light, and depicted in a light brown. Hung Jui-Lin is adept at the expression of light, and skilled in the use of color. Without superfluous strokes, this female nude is able to convey the warmth of human flesh using spare, precise lines. Though completed within a short span of time, each quick sketch is accomplished with brushwork that the artist has refined over a lifetime. There is much to savor within the small frame. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 4

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin’s depictions of the human form can be categorized as miners and female nudes. He once said, “Miners have bodies of intensive labor; the bodies of female nudes are elegant and supple.” The proud posture of this voluptuous female nude expresses the beauty of the human form. In addition to the ink lines, diluted ink has been applied as shading. The brightest areas on the periphery of the silhouette are depicted using the liubai (leaving blank) technique. From the image, one senses that the artist’s mood is tranquil and unperturbed while observing the human model. He practiced painting the rigid texture of plaster busts in his youth, and now must express the softness in the musculature and skin of the human body. After over 30 years of sketching the rugged, masculine bodies of miners, Hung Jui-Lin can quietly enjoy the joy of painting the model before him. This work reveals a calmness and ease. The artist does not repeat the simple brushstrokes and curves and subtly expresses the posture of a woman sitting atop a pedestal. Her gentle composure flows from the inked brush. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

listRow.content: This painting of a snowy scene was completed in 1966, when Hung Jui-Lin accompanied Li Mei-Shu and Shih Tsui-Feng on a visit to Japan to investigate the arts education system, visiting their classmate Hosoume on the way. The nimble, simple lines express the heavy layer of snow that covers the buildings, roads, and tree branches. The dark and hazy sky are like a curtain to the glistening world of whiteness, like an expansive scene being unveiled on the silver screen through a long lens. A solitary figure, carrying an umbrella and a wearing a maroon cloak, trudges through the snow, brings an element of unspoken narrative to the picture and adding a breath of culture. Head bowed, the pedestrian moves forward in the snow, conveying the bone chilling cold. This trip to Japan was made nearly three decades after he left Yamagata Prefecture in 1937. As always, Hung Jui-Lin rapidly captures the scene before him in the shortest time possible. The objects conveyed though liubai (leaving blank), the sky depicted using rendered ink, and the rapid simple lines in the work expresses the immediate atmosphere of the snowy scene, documenting the snowy country on the artist’s travels. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

listRow.content: While teaching at the Academy of Arts, men were invited to sit as models for sketching classes, but in much lower numbers than female models. In this work, the male model is posed seated in profile, leaning against the back of his chair. His muscles are lax, unlike the deformed tension of the miners’ due to over exertion. The exaggerated form of the miners’ bodies was a significant visual provocation for Hung Jui-Lin. Hung Jui-Lin has used a permanent marker to outline the silhouette of the human body and then used the side of a brush with dry ink to create the shadows in the nape of the neck, shoulder blades, and the left arm. The work is concise with few strokes, but Hung Jui-Lin remains focused and enthralled in being presented with a model. The miners in the colliery could not be still for Hung Jui-Lin to sketch in peace, but the artist’s emphasis was on the miners’ emotional state and collective atmosphere. When opposite a professional human model, Hung Jui-Lin reverts to simplicity and retrains his personal sentiments. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

title: Sketchbook 4
medium: Pencil, ink, and ballpoint pen on paper

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin completed this sketchbook while teaching at the National Taiwan Academy of Arts. He began teaching at the Academy of Arts in 1964, and this sketchbook was from his second year of teaching. He uses any implement on hand as his creative media, such as pencil, ink wash, ballpoint pens, etc. The year 1965 has been written on the cover. Hung Jui-Lin has numbered works up to 93, but his eldest daughter Hung Bai-Yun has recorded the number at 89. Hong Jui-Lin’s two daughters have helped to organize his works, making notations on the cover, but currently only 77 works are accounted for. The themes include the male body, female nudes, male and female students at the easels focused on painting nudes, as well as portraits of several male and female students. Students often serve as models too. The faithful portrayal of classes at the Academy of Arts (present day National Taiwan University of Arts) is a precious record. Hong Jui-Lin’s intimate interactions with his students and the convivial teaching atmosphere can be seen from this sketchbook. It also preserves the immediacy of Hung Jui-Lin’s sketches of the human form. Among the works is a sketch of a female nude above which the words “hard work, carefree, and craftsman” have been written, presumably because Hung Jui-Lin had explained to his students that the creative mood and aesthetic presentation differs when painting laborers and nudes, concepts he conveyed to his students. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

listRow.content: This quick sketch of a female nude was created in 1965 during the artist’s second year teaching at the Academy of Arts. Before class begins, Hung Jui-Lin would usually agree with the model on the pose he wishes them to take. After the students sketch for a while, he would begin surveying their work, suggesting to the students where issues might be and providing individual guidance, but he would not correct the painting for the student. This model has been depicted from the back. Her two arms are curved with her hands converging on the back of her head, as though adjusting her hair. It is an elegant pose. The model’s form has been outlined with precision using saturated ink lines. From the right arm down to the right shoulder, the right thigh and calf are all shaded and have been rendered with a thick brush and diluted ink. The lines of the spine and shoulder blades are lightly picked out with a fine brush. Rounded and weighty, the buttocks lead into the folded right leg. The overlapping of saturated and diluted hues convey light and shadows as well as a sense of interest. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Quick Sketch, Female Nude 2

listRow.content: In 1964, Hung Jui-Lin responded to an invitation from Li Mei-Shu, Director of the Department of Western Painting at the National Taiwan Academy of Arts, to teach there. Upon arriving at the National Taiwan Academy of Arts, he taught sketching for the Department of Sculpture and Department of Chinese Painting; and subsequently taught sketching, oil painting, and watercolors at the Department of Western Painting. He would sketch along with students when they sketched the human body, and completed these rapidly. Hence, there are quite a number of female nudes among the his surviving works. This work was completed during his second year at the National Taiwan Academy of Arts. The female figure is on one knee, with her right hand resting lightly on her knee, and her left hand resting on her hip. This pose is difficult to hold, and allows for little time to sketch. The lines of the human figure in the work are steady and precise, with the exception of a correction in the upper left arm and right calf. Despite being practiced, there are sometimes imperfections, but these do not take away from the expressiveness of the work. Dimensionality has been created using diluted ink in he left breast and the shaded parts of the body. The center of gravity in the buttocks and thighs underscore the sense of volume in this female nude. On a foundation of solid realism, Hung Jui-Lin has refined simple pivotal lines in his mastery of the form and posture of the female nude. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

title: Portrait of the Artist's Mother, Shih Yeh-liang

listRow.content:
Hung Jui-Lin’s mother Shi Yeh-Liang was born in 1880 in Taipei’s Monga. This water color portrait of her with a head of white hair at age 84 was painted by Hung Jui-Lin (then 52 years of age). His mother was the adopted daughter of a traditional Chinese medicine practitioner, and the second wife of Hung Jui-Lin’s father Hung Ho-Ting. She bore three children, including Hung Jui-Lin and his younger brother and sister.

Hung Jui-Lin first sketched using pencil, then applied water color in this depiction of his mother in profile. His depiction of his mother’s facial features are extremely realistic, with her wrinkled brow, sunken cheeks, and sagging neck revealing her advancing age, but the peaceful gaze conveys a serenity. With a flesh-toned base color, amber lines strengthen the dimensionality in her face and add to the realism of the figure as well as capture the subtle flashes of instantaneous change in lights and shadows. The texture of hairs strands in her white hair has been achieved through flying-white (kasuri) rubbing to create a mottled texture, and her clothing has been painted using freehand brushwork, placing an emphasis on the tranquility and detachment of the figure.  (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

listRow.content: Miners are soaked with perspiration after heavy manual labor, and yearn most for the cleansing and relaxation a hot bath in the communal bathing pool provides when they exit the pit. The miners strip down and gather around the bathing pool to wash away the coal dust, and share details from their work day and of mining conditions. This is the most enjoyable aspect after a day of toil. The women in charge of heating the water for the bath do so with hot coals, which makes the water temperature difficult to control with precision. If the water is not hot enough, or if temperatures fluctuate too drastically, they are often subjected to verbal abuse. Their indignant at the complaints may lead to altercations that cause them to walk out on the job. Chin S. Houng said, “Later we were able to employ an auntie to heat the water who stayed with us a long time because she was deaf and could not hear the insults.” This painting depicts five miners washing by the bathing pool, in individual poses. Some are toweling off, some washing their hair. Bathing miners is a frequent subject in Hung Jui-Lin’s paintings. It is extremely challenging as their movements shift quickly. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

title: A Glorious Summer Day in Paradise 1

listRow.Title: A Glorious Summer Day in Paradise 1

listRow.content: We often see works depicting miners hard at work in the darkness of the mineshaft, but this work portrays the emotional state of miners using crisp, clear tones. One senses the sense of peace Hung Jui-Lin was experiencing in that moment. The work reveals the imagery of the mine using a variety of elements. There is a pickaxe and bamboo scoop on the bottom left. The miner on the right rests his cheek on his hand, deep in thought. He is wearing rubber boots, with a packed lunch wrapped in a kerchief by his feet; on his head is a soft canvas hat and headlamp, he sits bored on planks of acacia wood. In the midground are three miners and two sections of minecarts. The overall imagery has an ethereal quality, with the central figure looming large and prominent. He is waiting to begin work, for the cart to bring them into the subterranean mineshafts. What thoughts course though his mind? What can be think of? The miners would often said, “Work, and I might die; don’t work, then my whole family may perish.” In that moment, he can only bravely enter the pit and battle once more. The elements in this work reveal the miner’s way of life. The demeanor of the miner is also emotive, conveying the indescribable savoring of life. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

title: Assembled and Waiting
medium: Ink and pigment on cotton paper

listRow.content: This group of miners seem to be gathered in wait for the minecart to bring them to the pit. Beginning with the figure on the far right dressed in a rain poncho, there are nine miners in two rows. The first and second miners on the right faces the viewer while the third miner has turned away. The remaining figures are gazing toward the light source. Bathed in light and casting a distinct shadow, this group of laborers impart a certain serenity. The positioning of the figures in a row also produces a sense of volume. The sight of a row of laborers and farmers standing in the wind and snow in 1937 impressed him with the farmer’s resilience in struggling against nature for survival, and sensed their serenity. Hung Jui-Lin once said, “the work of miners is sacred. I feel that it is Godly.” He also commented that, “I realize increasingly that the frank and unaffected expressions of miners correspond to my own spirit and compel me at every moment to capture them instantly with my paint brush.” The contrast of light and shadows in this work reveals the solemnity of the miners’ lives. They work hard, and put their lives on the line, prepared to make the ultimate sacrifice. They exemplify the glory of humanity. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

title: Waiting to Enter the Mine
medium: Ink and pigment on cotton paper

listRow.content: This work has been signed “礦山人 (Man from the Mountain Mines)” in Chinese. “Man from the Mountain Mines was a moniker Hung Jui-Lin gave himself. The Mountain Mines refers to the Huaishan Colliery where he worked, which was located in Longtan Mountain in Ruifang District. The concept of a living in a mountain hermitage is an aspiration for many refined literati. Having studied Western painting in Japan, Hung Jui-Lin’s father Hong He-Ting was refined and cultured, and excelled in both literature and art. Hung Jui-Lin’s childhood was steeped in the cultural heritage imparted by his father, and was especially drawn toward Chinese brush and ink painting and calligraphy. In 1957, Haishan Colliery excavated coal of an excellent quality and the number of miners working increased exponentially. Hence, Hung Jui-Lin focused on group portraits during this time. By 1959, the yield was nearing completion, and the group portraits omitted depictions of context, without distinctions between the mine adit or colliery yard. Miners are often depicted in a row without differentiating between foreground, mid-ground, or background. The outlines in this group portrait are relatively detailed, using both wet and dry brush, and renderings of saturated and diluted ink. The distinction between light and shade are exceptionally clear. The effects of the monochromatic quick sketch closely approach the expressions of traditional brush and ink painting. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

title: Preparing to Enter the Mine

listRow.content: From 1957 to 1960, Hung Jui-Lin created a series of group portraits of miners. Painting all types of scenes, seated, standing, conversing, waiting, entering the pit, exiting the pit. Every situation was deserving of Hung Jui-Lin preserving the image of these dedicated laborers. When miners gathered at spaces such as the mine adit or coal silo, perhaps allowed Huang Jui-Lin to portray them with more leisure. Those were the years when coal production was most prolific at the the Haishan Colliery, and operations at the colliery was especially busy, with an increased number of miners. This inspired Hung Jui-Lin to focus on groups of miners as a theme, and he became increasingly adept at managing group portraits. With flowing ink wash, this work depicts seven miners. An outline of the figures was first created using a fine brush and saturated ink, and then a diluted ink used to create folds and textures in the clothing. The scene has been illuminated from the right, hence the brightest point created through the liubai (leaving blank) technique is in the clothing of miners in the left foreground, while the four miners on the right are in the darkness, their heads bowed in silence. There is a tacit understanding between the miners in this tranquil scene. The group portrait demonstrates a spatial relationship of back, front, left and right. The seven miners mutually overlap in a linear space, without a mid-distance or far-distance. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

title: Sketchbook 3
medium: Ink, pigment, and pastel on paper

listRow.content: The first page of this sketchbook is dated January 25, 1958. It includes a total of 32 works. The contents include portraits of individual miners faces, one of whom had been injured on duty and lost his sight in one eye. A number of other works feature scenes of miners bathing, expressing the strength and beauty of the miners’ bodies. There are also numerous quick sketch portraits. All of the figures are friends and colleagues of Hung Jui-Lin. Additionally, there are scenes from within the mine pit, such as miners waiting for the minecart, groups of mine workers waiting to enter the pit or gathered around the stove in the dormitory to keep warm, team discussions before entering the pit to work – all scenes from the daily lives of miners. These sketches often depict the same scene twice, either from a slightly different angles, or with or without the application of color. These works can be regarded as pure practice. Though Hung Jui-Lin’s had achieved a level of refinement in his painting by this time, he persisted in painting this way each day. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Sketchbook 3

tfam.Media Technology: Ink, pigment, and pastel on paper

listRow.content: This sketchbook was created in 1958. Perhaps due to Hung Jui-Lin’s position, he personally inspected every corner of the colliery. There are 29 works in this sketchbook that record various jobs and tasks performed by miners. A number of these depict timbermen repairing props in the mines. Timbermen were paid according to the length in meters of new props made. The same is true for repairing old wooden structures in the pit. Hewers are paid according to the weight of the coal collected (a cart equals a ton). These three categories of miners all work in the pit. The sketchbook includes eight individual portraits, the others are group portraits featuring two or three miners in scenes of making repairs, chatting, or keeping warm. Hung Jui-Lin said, “The colliery is a highly sophisticated operation. Carts, pickaxes, props and beams, ventilation. Each requires technical knowledge.” For thirty-five years, he depicted all types of miners without fail, seemingly drawing inexhaustible insight in the process. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Sketchbook 2

listRow.content: There are 25 quick studies in this sketch book, with 32 pages handwritten by Hung Jui-Lin. As there are works that take up a single page, are double-sided, or span several pages, hence there are 25 works in total. Five of the works are scenes of miners settling their wages at the business office; seven works depict miners erecting the timber frame in the mine pit. The construction of the wooden mineshafts is arduous work, involving complex civil engineering calculations and carpentry skills to determine the length and shape of the supporting acacia wood according to the topography inside the pit. Three of the sketches are quick studies of portraits of individual miners using pure lines, one of which stands out for featuring a female errand runner. The remaining works are group portraits of miners that document the daily lives of miners in the colliery, and resting in the dormitories. Two works portray miners seated in mine carts, and one work features a scene of miners waiting for a cart to take them out of the mines. Many works in the sketchbook feature themes of work in the mines and attests to Hung Jui-Lin’s comment that he brought the simplest of media into the pit to draw: a sketchbook, a bamboo brush, and a film cannister full of ink. There are numerous works in the sketchbooks that provide references to the inner workings of the coalmine. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Sketchbook 1

title: Group Portrait at the Mine Entrance
medium: Ink and pigment on cotton paper

listRow.content: Miners work deep underground every day and witness the fragility of life. Each time the gather at the adit to the mine, and pass through the requisite inspection process, an inexplicable pressure begins to foment. The light blue areas on the painting hint at the adit to the mine. This is the boundary between darkness and light, as well as the line that demarcates the battle between life and death. Hung Jui-Lin places an emphasis on capturing light and forms. He uses soft, gentle brushwork to draw out the physical forms of the miners, and applies a tint of light brown. The liubai (leaving blank) treatment on the shoulders indicates where the light falls. The contrast between light blue and light brown is rarely seen and diverges from the usual applications of ink and amber. This is perhaps a depiction of miners gathering near the adit at dawn, before entering the pit. A sense of anxiety pervades before entering the pit. Most of the miners have their heads bowed in silence as they resign themselves to the unpredictable future and make their way into the mineshaft to excavate coal. The lithe, liberated brush and ink incongruously outline the weighty bodies of the miners on paper. Their physical forms are connected by color and ink, like fates intertwined. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Group Portrait at the Mine Entrance

tfam.Media Technology: Ink and pigment on cotton paper

listRow.content: Like a photographer, Hung Jui-Lin seizes on each fleeting moment in order to preserve scenes he witnesses at the mines. He captures the dynamism of the miners, paints their momentary movements as though pressing a shutter to crystalize an instant. The brightest point in the painting is the white strip representing the long bench in the miners’ dormitory. Three miners are seated firmly on the bench, perhaps resting or waiting, without interacting with one another. Hung Jui-Lin depicts the three silent miners in varying poses. The figure on the right rests both hands on the back of his head; the figure in the center rests one leg on the other; and the figure on the left is shirtless, revealing a slightly sagging torso and his neck retracted. The three are proportionally balanced in the painting. Their thighs and the edge of the bench are illuminated, while the area under the bench is the darkest. By depicting the shadows cast by the figures’ legs, there is a distinction between light and shadow in the shaded areas, which creates a natural spatial expression. Hung Jui-Lin said, “I do not intend to place an emphasis on anything. Whether the dead, the elderly, or those in the prime of health, miners would definitely not wish to intentionally make a statement about their way of life.” Hung Jui-Lin never intentionally depicts miners in grand gestures. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Three Miners on a Bench

title: Teams of Threes and Fours Chatting

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin painted a number of group portraits with coal silos as setting in 1957 and 1958, the most productive years for the Haishan Colliery. On careful inspection, no two of the miners under his brush have the same pose or movement. The subject of this group portrait are the four people conversing. They are seated on acacia wood planks, their relative positions and interactive expressions are unclear, but the sense that they are conversing is thoroughly conveyed. The man in shorts on the far right with his back to the viewer is holding a pickaxe. His relaxed posture is reminiscent of that in a life drawing. The three on the left are also seated on acacia wood planks. Their eyes look blankly ahead. Besides the mutual response, and the relative positions between the bodies in space, the treatment in this group portrait seems like a radiation of power, with the characters on the left and right gazing off to the left and right respectively. Through his keen sense of observation, and precise brushwork, Hung Jui-Lin organizes the otherwise chaotic characters. The expression of group portraits is difficult to grasp without skills honed over time. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Teams of Threes and Fours Chatting

listRow.content: Two minecarts filled with miners have been juxtaposed in this work. In the cart on the left, a figure stands with a pickaxe over his shoulder. In the foreground, three men in long trousers stand next to the minecarts, two are in shorts. One of the men in trousers with his hands in his pockets is presumably an inspector. An inspector would enter the pit and perform safety checks. Miners would only enter the pit after inspectors give confirmation. Supervisors would also repeat safety precautions and warn miners not to bring cigarettes or alcohol into the pit. In this work, the miners in the mine carts have been presented in symbolic form. The clothing of those standing outside the cart have been depicted using different colors. The use of intermediate tones add to the somber atmosphere. The overall tones in the work are solemn. All of the workers are fully clothed, perhaps the painting was undertaken before dawn on a winter’s day. The painting does not display the hurried lines seen in the works from inside the pit, and the backdrop and ground have been painted flat with color. Bright areas of illumination have been left on the caps of the figures, the mine cart, and on the ground. Hung Jui-Lin’s outline of a scene before miners enter the pit combines group portrait with narrative. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Waiting to Enter the Mine

listRow.content: The nature of mining requires heavy manual labor and a monotonous daily routine as well as a constant state of tension. In order to alleviate tension, miners would invite good friends for drinks or to gamble after leaving the mine as a way to relieve stress. In this work, miners are squatting, sitting, or standing, with the majority directing their gaze toward a group seated in a circle at the center; there is a cohesive directional gaze. The dozen or so figures are in varying poses, and the positioning of the figures within the scene creates a sense of layering. The miners are staggered in height. It is a richly rhythmic group portrait. The group portraits of miners emerged after the portraits of individual miners, and the emphasis is no longer on the expression of individual images, but in expressing the relationship in the mutual resonance within a collective. Some are engaged in conversation, others turn their heads to look back, and others have their backs to the audience, or have their heads bowed in thought, as well as yet others seated on the ground. Hung Jui-Lin lithely sketches using brush and ink, omitting the detailed depiction of facial expressions, and applies the same color to all the miners. His brush work and color application is simple and honest, which corresponds with the image of the miners. The foreground and distant background have been omitted in this painting, but great importance is given to the expression of light, as the sense of three-dimensionality and texture would be lost without light and shadows. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Placing Wagers

listRow.content:
Hung Jui-Lin uses ink wash and diluted colors in his miner paintings. He once said, “My father left behind a lot of good rice paper. It was a pity to leave it lying around so I decided to try it. The mines are a colorless place, which was perfect for showcasing the allure of ink. My father used to enjoy using ink, and as I age, I have grown to feel that the color of ink approaches brown, both modest and unadorned. When they are used well, they can be more emotive than color.”

There were some 200 miners at the Haishan Colliery. Hung Jui-Lin captures their way of life in the short period when the miners gather, and completes the paintings with brushwork of varying point size and saturation and slight rendering. The visual scope of this work is expansive, with Sanjua Mountain in the distance. Hung Jui-Lin is positioned at the office, facing the distant mountain, with a view of the colliery full of miners. The depiction of the large number of miners documents an golden era at the Haishan Colliery. Leaning against a cart with his arms crossed, the figure at the center of the painting is the focal point, like a character on stage. The remaining figures have their backs to the viewer. The miners bear witness to the scenes of prosperity at the colliery. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Miners Gathering

listRow.content: “For coalminers, not seeing the light of day is not a mere description, but an accurate reflection of their reality. They enter the pit before dawn breaks, and if they are fortunate enough to come out of the pit at the end of the workday, the sun has already set.” Hung Jui-Lin developed a steadfast mutual partnership with fellow coalminers over his years of working alongside them. These laborers otherwise unknown to the world have been preserved in the hearts of the people in another form. Miners develop solid muscles through manual labor, which become deformed through overuse in elderly miners as they age. Using ink-wash lines, Hung Jui-Lin captures the image of the hunched back and deformed joints in this elderly miner; then highlights the textures of human musculature in rendered light colors. From 1957. Hung Jui-Lin no longer detailed or emphasized the visual appearance of individual miners so individual miners cannot be identified; he gradually moved toward shaping a universal image of minors. The figure and motion of a minor painted on the front and reverse sides of this work are similar, and appear to be the same miner. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Old Miner

listRow.content: This errand runner wears a bamboo hat to shade against the sun because his work is outside of the mine pit. In his depiction, the turns in Hung Jui-Lin’s lines are especially strong, rough, and forceful. Overlapping lines depict his face, elbows, and knees, with a flavor suggestive of Georges Rouault’s human silhouettes traced in heavy black lines. Color has been brushed onto the figure's body, and his blue shirt and shorts have been completed in simple strokes. His serious expression carries a hint of sadness. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Worker Wearing Bamboo Hat

title: Sketchbook 5
medium: Ink, pen, and pigment on paper

listRow.content: In the era before sketchbooks existed, Hung Jui-Lin purchased tailor notebooks for sketches because the pages were blank and unlined that allowed for painting. These were the notebooks that he brought into the mines. If he ran out of ink, he would mix coal dust with sweat and dirt and paint with that. A label on the cover of this notebook says “self-portraits” but there are no self-portraits inside. The majority of the 21 works contained were works in pencil and markers in November 1971 of scenes of timbermen carrying out maintenance work, piles of acacia wood and the long, deep drifts and shafts in the mines. The sketchbook exemplifies Hung Jui-Lin statement that the mine pit was his studio, and that in his eyes, miners were comparable to Michelangelo’s statues. Dynamic group portraits of miners are always presented using powerful ink lines under his brush. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
