title: The Death Indicates What Our Life Is

listRow.Title: The Death Indicates What Our Life Is

title: Miners Waiting to Enter the Mine in a Mining Car

listRow.content: The miners seated or standing in the minecart prepare to enter the mine. Each miner is wearing a canvas cap equipped with a headlamp. The figure on the far right with his arms across his chest leans against the edge of the cart, still wearing his coat. The figure with his back to the viewer has already removed his shirt and trousers. As soon as all the miners are settled in this line (usually six) of minecarts, they will all enter the mines together. Entering the mine each day is a battle between life and death, with the potential for unexpected situations and a deep fear of accidents. There is a pervasive sense of anxiety, and the facial expressions are somber. The source of light in the painting originates from the right foreground. The artist has chosen to paint the figures in one particular cart. The miners are positioned in different heights; some in profile, others with their back to the viewer. The wooden frame of the mine cart binds this team of miners and creates the sense of space. Recording a scene at the colliery with his paint brush, Hung Jui-Lin always provides room for the viewer’s imagination beyond the painting. These characters have numerous internal monologues. Hung Jui-Lin’s understanding of them enables him to be rapid, steadfast, intuitive in his brush and ink expression, while preserving the atmosphere of the moment. The background of brown and dark cyan brushstrokes blended in different directions has the same tonality as the human figures. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Miners Waiting to Enter the Mine in a Mining Car

title: Chatting and Resting outside the Mine

listRow.content: In this work, thick, dark lines are used to depict the forms of the miners. There is some overlap in the lines that shape their faces, hats, headlamps and limbs, and the brushwork expresses the rugged, straightforward characteristic of miners. Georges Rouault’s thick, dark outlines of the human silhouette had a strong influence on Hung Jui-Lin. The form of the second miner from the right with a flask in his hand has been outlined in thick, saturated lines. His large eyes and sunken cheeks highlight the image of the miners. His strong, prominent calves are the result of long-term laboring. His gaze is directed toward miners on his left, seemingly describing an event to the other three who stare blankly ahead. Many miners have such speechless expressions under Hung Jui-Lin’s brush. In addition to the main subjects of the four miners in the foreground, there are a group of miners in the far distance, in upper right corner of the painting, who give depth to the scene. This work was painted in 1957, which was a bumper year for the Haishan Colliery. Prior to this, the Haishan Colliery had been deemed a failed mine by assessors, and the Ni family was on the eve of abandoning mining efforts. Fortunately, the mine yielded coal this particular year. The miners must have been especially busy. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Chatting and Resting outside the Mine

listRow.content: This work depicts a scene from the operations in the mines. There are three layers to the work. In the foreground, three miners are waiting for work to continue, they sit on the acacia wood poles either with their eyes closed in rest, or looking off into the distance. The figure sitting on the right seems to be suddenly conscious of being the subject of a sketch, and turns to glance at the artist. Moments where the subject exchanges a glance with the artist are often seen in Hung Jui-Lin’s work. Standing behind those seated in the foreground are five figurative miners in different poses and orientations, and in the far distance are a laborer pushing a cart full of acacia wood as well as three mine carts full of miners. Hung Jui-Lin is adept at documenting such routine and busy scenes of miners at work. He is able to capture the gesture of a human figure within a short span of time, and accurately depicts the bodily movements of miners even in the far distance. Hung Jui-Lin’s miner portraits are valued because they bear witness to Taiwan’s miners. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Distributing Wood in the Mine

listRow.content:
Despite the difficulties in depicting the miners’ environment, the collective action of miners was profoundly moving to Hung Jui-Lin and provided an endless stream of creative impetus. This work depicts miners eating out of their bento boxes. Two miners, one seated and one standing, bento box in hand, focus their attention on their lunches. They seize an available moment to fill their stomachs wherever they find themselves in the colliery. They are resigned to this daily occurrence. Scenes such as this one conveys the ways in which miners are persevering laborers who adjust to their environments. Hung Jui-Lin outlines the figures with a thick, saturated brush to capture the scene.
Temperatures are high inside the pit, making it necessary for miners to strip down in order to work, as evident in this work. Miners often take their meals in the time waiting for the mine carts ferrying the coal out of the mines to return. They eat in the relatively more spacious area where the shafts and drifts intersect. Eating in the pit takes place in darkness except for the light provided by their headlamps. If they have a opportune moment outside the pit, they can more comfortably take their meal wherever they find a suitable place to do so. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Eating

listRow.content: The miners depicted by Hung Jui-Lin are without an ounce of pretense. They don’t understand Hung Jui-Lin’s reasons for drawing them. Hung Jui-Lin has said that he relies on intuition when he paints. He is also an frank and unpretentious person. Even a miner picking his ear has been depicted honestly. The four miners in the front row seem to have a spot light on them. The row of figures in behind them stand in the dim shade. The two in the left foreground are clothed, while the two on the right are shirtless. They are seated on the same bench, each with a distinct movement. The expression on their faces is stony and genuine, expressing the miners’ sense of ennui and anticipation. Hung Jui-Lin has always insisted on painting the lives of miners because they are authentic and kind. They are authentic in their honesty toward others; and kind in their dedication and work ethic. They are cooperative, and uncomplaining. They are without selfish intentions in doing work that benefits others, this serious attitude toward life is an expression of goodness. This work expresses a theatrical effect with figures in the foreground and crowds in the background. Everyone looks somber, but viewers might be able to hear a wordless miner’s song. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Four Miners on a Bench

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin said, “My paintings of miners beginning from what is ‘authentic’ and ‘good.’ Authenticity is sincere, unpretentious. That is the life of a miner – very straightforward, innocent, without pretense.” This was the impetus behind Hung Jui-Lin’s persistent portray of miners. There are six miners depicted in this work. Five are seated in two facing rows, as though conversing and killing time. Though their expressions are blurred, the postures and gestures of the figures impart an atmosphere of respite. The last person in the row on the left sits in a direction opposite from the rest and is not a part of this group engaged in conversation. The solitary miner, deep in thought, is a sight often seen. There is a pickaxe in the hand of the miner wearing white and squatting on the ground to the left of the front row. The pickaxe is a personal tool. There is a sack next to the miner wearing blue and hugging his knees on the right. As he is closest to the artist, his thick brows and large eyes have been depicted. The blue-shirted miner and the solitary miner in the distance vary greatly in the size, indicating spatial distance within the work. As with many group portraits of seated or squatting miners, this work has a single background color and does not depict a specific setting. Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Chatting outside the Mine

listRow.content: This work exemplifies the classic style of the artist’s group portraits of miners, depicting three main subjects in the foreground, and a group of miners in the near distance. The work stands apart for the three miners in the foreground wearing yellow, green, and red – an inspired departure from Hung Jui-Lin’s usual amber and ink tones. Beside the miner wearing red in the foreground are three barrel-shaped water flasks with caps – aluminum water flasks used by miners in the 1950s. The miner has his back to the viewer, with his flask across his shoulder, the headlamp wire winds across his shoulder and is plugged into the battery pack around his waist. Miners and mine carts scatter in the back row. They are busy preparing for entry into the pit. The color scheme helps to establish distance in this work. Mineral colors in yellow, green, and red on the three men in the foreground add to the vitality of the painting. The grayish blue hues of the mine carts and miners standing in the backgrounds are akin to the backdrop in stage design, set apart from the focal point. The busy and repetitive life trajectory forms the life rhythm day after day, this was Hung Jui-Lin’s hymn to the miner. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Waiting to Start Work

title: Waiting in front of the Office

listRow.content: The daily procedure for miners begins at the office wall where two name badges for each miner are hung. They take one card to the charging station and exchange it for a headlamp and batteries. Then, they bring their equipment to the inspection room where they handover flammable items such as cigarettes and lighters to the inspector. The other card is left on the wall to indicate that the individual has entered the pit. In this work, numerous miners have gathered outside the timber office building. The miners are not wearing their battery packs. There is a water flask and a pickaxe on the ground on the left, suggesting that the miners have gathered in front of the office as they await the distribution of battery packs. This work is a treatment of relationships within a group portrait. Each of the dozen or so miners differ in their clothing, the angle and position of their stances, their action and pose. On the one hand, the work conveys the grandeur of throngs of laborers, on the other hand, it realistically depicts the actual space. The characters and architecture have been deftly outlined with a wet brush, the light and shade mastered in the rendering of color, the brightest areas are in the eaves and on the ground. The atmosphere of preparation before entry into the pit comes alive on paper. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Waiting in front of the Office

title: Miners Waiting to Exit the Mine
medium: Pastel, ink, and pigment on paper

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin said, “I used the simplest methods of expression to paint. I filled a canister that came with a roll of camera film with ink, and dipped my brush in it to paint. This was the simplest way. I had nothing else on me except a brush and a small container of ink. This was enough to express my heart’s intentions.” Working in the high temperatures of the dark mine pit, the miners in this work are in the nude. Two are seated, and two are standing; their faces are blackened by coal dust. Neither excavating nor mining, they gaze at the narrow mine shaft, quietly listening for the sound of mine carts, anticipating its arrival from the depths of the shaft to ferry the coal they have collected or to take them out of the pit. Of the four miners, the two on the left are in profile, the two on the right have their back to the viewer. They are illuminated by the artist’s headlamp. Hung Jui-Lin outlines the strong, sturdy form of their bodies using overlapping lines. A rarely seen vibrant blue and violet is used in this work to express the light inside the mine pit, which highlights the warm tones of the human bodies. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Miners Waiting to Exit the Mine

tfam.Media Technology: Pastel, ink, and pigment on paper

title: Anxiety before Entering the Mine
medium: Ink and pigment on cotton paper

listRow.content: The group portraits of miners often depict a dozen or so miners. Hung Jui-Lin always positioned himself in close proximity in sketching these laborers. The miners are relatively static before the enter the mine pit, but they are shrouded in a certain atmosphere. The person sitting on the right covers his face as though weeping, or perhaps as a result of exhaustion. The others seem solemn or expressionless. Even those who are standing, have their eyes closed in thought. No one meets the artist’s gaze. They seem to be coping with a certain difficulty, and are unable or unwilling to think, repressing their emotions instead. This atmosphere expresses the aspect of miners that is resigned to their destiny. This evoked concern and compassion in Hung Jui-Lin. The miners’ heads, bodies, and clothing have been sketched and filled using heavy ink lines and a single uniform color. A few strokes of diluted color on the ground are the miners’ shadows. The background has been created using a dry brush, as though shrouded in a haze. The group portrait emphasizes the resonant relationship between the many figures, which is revealed in this work. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Anxiety before Entering the Mine

tfam.Media Technology: Ink and pigment on cotton paper

listRow.content: This work depicts a team of miners gathered at the pit adit before the break of day, to discuss their work assignment upon entering the pit. Two miners are engaged in discussion at the center of the work, while the man standing across from them is bowed in silence. The figure on the far right appears nonchalant. The tall miner on the left is fully engaged, while the one on the far left appears distracted. This is perhaps a routine daily event which does not require full attention. Hung Jui-Lin’s depicts the group from an elevated perspective, hence, the silhouettes of the figures appear sturdy and stout with relatively short legs. The perspective in this work is from a much closer range than most group portraits. The three miners in the foreground are portrayed in profile, their form outlined in thick brushstrokes of saturated ink. Their silhouettes are vivid and prominent. The abundant use of ink in this work creates a somber effect. Amber and dark green water color have been applied to the miners’ forms, with effects of light indicated using the liubai (leaving blank) technique to create a contrast of light and darkness. This group portrait of masculine miners reveals a sense of unease and doubt, and an atmosphere of pressure and foreboding. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Discussing

listRow.content:
Front:
Miners often draw deep on their cigarettes before the enter and after the exit the pit. They close their eyes and profoundly sense their existence, releasing any pressures. In their subconscious, this is like their last cigarette on earth, and an existential affirmation. Of the two laborers sitting on the acacia wood in the foreground, the man in the white shirt on the right is puffing clouds of smoke, while the one on the left sits silently in a stupor with his work tool beside him. The nature of this tool is difficult to determine based on appearance. Senior miners have suggested that this is a saw that had just been sharpened. It has been wrapped in paper to avoid injury in the process of bringing it into the pit. This dazed and distant expression is often seen among figures in Hung Jui-Lin’s paintings.

Back:
Miners sit around the colliery, chatting or in a daze. Scattered around an open area, they have a moment of respite. Hung Jui-Lin is able to capture these scenes by either standing with his sketchbook resting on a minecart, or seated with the sketchbook on his knees. Specific communication with the miners is not required. He presents an authentic image of life and work of the miners in an unaffected atmosphere. There are three miners seated in the foreground who are not interacting; three miners stand in the background as embellishment. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Preparing for Work

title: Waiting for News at the Mine Entrance
medium: Crayon, ink, and pigment on paper

listRow.content: This scene depicting a close, overlapping arrangement of miners is unique. The arched portal at the distance is the adit to a mine pit at Haishan Colliery. The miners are turned toward the pit adit, and make their way toward it. The crowd walk across the mine cart rails that wind toward the foreground from the right of the painting. Though the event depicted is unclear, the atmosphere is somber. Miners risk their lives each day in order to make a living. Accidents occur several times a year. These are devastating moments for Hung Jui-Lin, who has said that he cannot bear to, nor would he ever, depict these scenes of tragedy. This is perhaps scene of miners gathering to begin work, but a group portrait depicting such crowds is unusual. The human figures, the rails, and piles of acacia wood have been sketched using pastel crayons. The silhouettes of miners in the furthest, darkest distance are shaded using dark gray pastel crayon, graduating to a grayish blue. The areas with the most light have been depicted using liubai (leaving blank). The work is spare in its use of brush and ink, and colors have been applied using charcoal and pastel crayon. Diluted ink has been applied with a large brush for the sky and ground. This is a work that piques the curiosity. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Waiting for News at the Mine Entrance

tfam.Media Technology: Crayon, ink, and pigment on paper

title: Planting and Building Together
medium: Crayon and pigment on cotton paper

listRow.content:
This setting for this work is similar to that of Cleaning the Coal Storage Area, which also depicts a scene of errand runners at work. But these workers are working to move soil with hoes. The figure in the center in a skirt and gloves is a woman intently at work on raking through the dirt mound. The shirtless figure on the far-right shoulders a yoke, waiting to carry a load. They are presumably working to remove the rubble from the mound. This painting seems to tell a story, perhaps the miners are working together to build a new home or prepare a new vegetable patch outside of their work at the mines. Hence, men and women are working together. 

The life of a miner is grueling, but their spirit of helping one another expresses a positive aspect of human nature. The human figures in the work have been outlined using pastel crayons to impart a sense of strength to the momentum of excavation, followed by an application of diluted ink and water color. The liubai (leaving blank) used in the figure wearing the coolie hat gives consideration to the layering. The four figures in the foreground are undertaking major physical labor, and his depiction is affirmative. The figure in the furthest distance seems to be doing the same. Hung Jui-Lin is adept at depicting the human body in motion. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Planting and Building Together

tfam.Media Technology: Crayon and pigment on cotton paper

listRow.content: Perhaps no one would describe the miners under Hung Jui-Lin’s brush as beautiful. He portrays them squatting on the ground at rest, laying in the coal seams at work, or seated with expressions of hopelessness and anxiety. This work depicts four miners sitting on the ground at rest. Their forms of the dark and powerful silhouettes are outlined, with their bodies and muscles in concise, forceful diluted ink and ochre. There is no background or base color, simply an image of a collective of four human male bodies, each in individual poses and actions, creating spatial definition through their relative positions. The ambiguity of whether the bodies created with smudged thick strokes are clothed or shirtless is not an issue. Hung Jui-Lin said, “Miners covered in coal dust, mud, and sweat are prototypes of beauty, like Michelangelo’s sculptures.” This is how he views the bodies of the miners around him, and the colliery became his art studio. The miners provided an inexhaustible stream of subject matter and varying forms of expression over the 35 years he spent on the colliery. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Chatting near the Mine

listRow.content: This work represents a expression of group portraiture, but the setting is not at the pit adit, nor is it in the pre-dawn when workers prepare to enter the mines. The miners sit in small groups around the colliery to rest or converse. There is a relative ease in the atmosphere compared to the groups standing in preparation to begin work. The three miners in the painting are seated on a cross made of acacia wood. There is a mine cart in the distance that might have just exited the pit. On the left, is a man standing deep in thought with his hands crossed behind his back, and a group of miners in conversation seated on the ground. The figures intersect horizontally and vertically against the vibrant green background. This type of composition with lively, pleasing saturated colors is rare among Hung Jui-Lin’s miner paintings. The acacia wood stored in the colliery lends a balancing effect to the painting. The choice of angle extends the spatial depth. Large numbers of acacia wood in varying lengths and girth are often scattered around the colliery. They are necessary for constructing support props in the pits, as well as required as sleepers for laying the minecart tracks. Like the minecart, they are a symbol of the colliery. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Waiting on Timber Supports

listRow.content: Before work begins inside the pit, the foreman or team leader would reiterate reminders to the miners to not bring alcohol or cigarettes and to be attentive to personal safety as well as ensure the safety of others. Despite the daily warnings, some miners still disregard the regulations. The haphazard attitude could easily lead to tragedy. The two miners in profile with their backs to the viewer stand facing four other miners, perhaps exhorting precautions. The miner in the foreground who appears the largest because he is closest to the artist is wearing long trousers. He is perhaps an administrative supervisor who will not be entering the pit to work. The artist is skilled in portraying varying expressions without depicting identifying features to the characters. Though this was a daily routine, it was done with care. The scene has been illuminated by the headlamp on the miner on the right, so the back of the miner in the right foreground is the darkest area of the painting, while the four figures on the left are illuminated. The light is the soul of Hung Jui-Lin’s miner paintings, and often results in an effect similar to stage lighting that invigorates the scene. This ray of light is also a foreshadowing of the light seen before entering the pit, with the anticipation of seeing the light once again upon exiting the pit. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Reminders before Entering the Mine

title: Greetings
medium: Ink and pigment on cotton paper

listRow.content: Before entering the pit to work, miners line up to collect their name badges and batteries for their headlamps, as well as a number for the minecart. Miners have an opportunity to chat in the time waiting to process the numerous registration procedures. Two miners in the foreground of this work are conversing. Between them is a group of miners whose size gradually decrease with distance, with two minecarts at the vanishing point. Hung Jui-Lin rarely painted realistic portraits of individual miners after 1957, and pivoted toward scenic group portraits of miners. We can no longer identify the individual miners he has depicted; these were replaced by scenes of miner collectives engaged in specific activities. The relationship between specific figures and the composition of the group portrait reveals on canvas the various events unfolding in the colliery. During this period, Hung Jui-Lin used his practiced, saturated brush to indulge in the depiction of all that he thinks and observes. Free and unfettered, he transformed ordinary scenes of daily life into a painterly realm rich with narrative depth. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Greetings

tfam.Media Technology: Ink and pigment on cotton paper

title: Vacant Stare
medium: Ink and pigment on cotton paper

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin knew the more than 200 miners at Huaishan Colliery by name, and was aware of their personalities, as well as their family and mining backgrounds. He was deeply involved in the lives of miners and hence was able to portray their uniqueness. This miner sits curled up, hugging his knees close. His coaldust covered face and clothing appear dirty, offsetting his wide eyes that gaze intently ahead, but what lies ahead? Through his portrait, the viewer senses the sadness, helplessness, and humility of the character. This also illustrates Hung Jui-Lin aesthetical view: what is beautiful or ugly is not in the appearance, but is in the power exuded by reality which provokes the human capacity for contemplation. Excavation in the mines often require explosives that cause coal dust and dirt to plume. Miners are often covered in coal dust when they first exit the mine pit, leaving only the white of their eyes and teeth untouched by the blackness. This miner’s facial expression sets him apart from others and triggers the viewer’s sympathy: what is he thinking of? Has he endured something unspeakable? (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Vacant Stare

tfam.Media Technology: Ink and pigment on cotton paper

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin used paintings instead of words to describe his miner friends. Whether in his portraits of groups of three or five miners, or the interaction between groups of portraits, Hung Jui-Lin hopes to capture moving silhouettes of his colleagues. There are ordinary people who suffer from various hardships behind these portraits. While painting them, Hung Jui-Lin also reflects on the value of his own life. This is the true meaning of art. Hung Jui-Lin is deeply moved by the kind nature, diligent attitude, and true heart of the miners. The essence of art is in the pursuit of “authenticity,” and miners are most able to express the authenticity of human nature. This miner is honest and innocent. Those who do not understand miners speak of an unattractiveness of form. The miner in the painting is a character with a strong body, and a image of patience, simplicity, and kindness. He is seated on a long bench, wearing only shorts. His two hands are crossed, as are his feet. He is unposed, in this everyday scene. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Miner Resting

title: Standing Miner
medium: Ink and pigment on cotton paper

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin’s full-length portrait of a single miner was inspired by sentiment that miners are laborers dedicated to the public good. They may appear rough and unattractive but their hearts are pure and true, revealing the nobility of human nature. This miner must have been invited by Hung Jui-Lin to stand at attention as a model for his sketch. He wears a hat and headlamp on his head, and a knotted towel around his neck. Dressed in shorts and barefooted, this is the typical style of a miner. He has a sturdy male physique with broad shoulders, the muscles of his chest, arms and legs are revealed in the artist’s flowing lines. His face suggests that he is of a certain age, but his solid body enables him to continue to rely on the labor of his body to make a living. Hung Jui-Lin is adept at capturing the human form and image. He once wrote: “I am inexplicably moved in the face of their solid and exhausted bodies, their unconcealed bare flesh and bones. I could almost touch the radiance of life beneath the skin covered by a concoction of dust and sweat.” He intended to paint portrait of miners that were religious, monumental, and sublime. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Standing Miner

title: Quietly Waiting to Enter the Mine
medium: Ink and pigment on cotton paper

listRow.content:
The number of group portraits of miners by the artist grew after 1955, and a gradual signature style emerged. On the whole, group portraits focused on the relationships between miners and their movements and gestures, and require a different organizational and arrangement skill compared to the portrayal of individual miners. Why did the group portraits emerge? Hung Jui-Lin had many opportunities to encounter gatherings of miners each day, which prompted him to develop his series of group portraits of miners. After more than a decade working at the colliery, Hung Jui-Lin had mastered the form of the miner. His lines were precise and flowing, his brush work rigorous, with very little retouching.

Whether shirtless, or fully dressed, straight on, in profile, or from behind, the bodies of the figures overlap and intersect, but there is a musicality in their staggered positions, and a rhythm to the complexity of the position and direction of their heads and feet. Their facial features have been simplified, with an emphasis on depicting the atmosphere and the lights and shadows. The background and setting have been omitted to focus on pure artistic expression. Thus, a distinctive style was established for Hung Jui-Lin’s group portraits of miners. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Quietly Waiting to Enter the Mine

tfam.Media Technology: Ink and pigment on cotton paper

title: Picking up Coal at the Mine Site

listRow.content: Toiling for life’s basic sustenance, miners rarely contemplate their future goals or life’s meaning. Their contributions to society are deserving of gratitude, because their work benefits everyone in society and are compensated only with enough for their families’ subsistence. The two workers on the left of this work stand in profile, shouldering an yoke with bamboo scoops suspended on each end, ostensibly for ferrying goods. The hunched figure in the foreground is struggling to shovel gravel into the bamboo scoop with his rounded shovel, while the figure standing on the right leans on his shovel, resting for a moment while waiting to take over from his colleague. Presumably, this is a scene of tidying up. Such scenes of labor are continuously enacted before Hung Jui-Lin’s eyes. They may not be miners, but they also exert physical labor and sweat as dedicated laborers which moves the artist. The rough brushstrokes, the heavy saturated ink lines of the figures, and the agile sophistication of the color application in this painting thoroughly and vividly expresses the exertion of the laborers within a short time frame. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Picking up Coal at the Mine Site

title: Cleaning the Coal Storage Area
medium: Ink and pigment on cotton paper

listRow.content: None of the miners in this painting are wearing miner’s caps except for the ones behind the minecart, indicating that they are datallers. They are consolidating coal cinder and rock spoil with shovels and rakes into a mound to the left of the painting. A figure stands to catch his breath, others are hard at work clearing the way to facilitate other operations at the colliery. They are not miners, but this work is also labor intensive. Hung Jui-Lin is compelled to sketch the various groups of laborers he encounters each day, as his artistry become increasingly refined from the way he handles his tools, applies force, configures the position and posture of each figure. He once put forward his view on the work of miners: “In the monotonous rhythm of the pickaxe, what cannot be denied is that they are mining not for coal but the essence of life.” Miners toil by silently exchanging their labor and life for money needed for life necessities, and to raise their children. For an artist working in the colliery, the perseverance, courage, sacrifice, sincerity, and honesty of the miners inspired Hung Jui-Lin to paint them over the course of thirty-five years. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

title: Miss Zhang Mei-Yao
