title: Various Forms of the 'Deer' Character over 4000 Years

listRow.Title: Various Forms of the 'Deer' Character over 4000 Years

listRow.content: The pickaxe is the tool primarily used by coalminers. Made of iron, the pickaxe can have two pointed ends, or a flat end and a pointed end, with an oval hole at the center through which a wooden handle can be inserted. In order to maintain its sharp edge worn away by the daily impact of coalmining, miners bring their pickaxes to the metal shop where they heat the blade over red hot coals before they exit the pits to bathe. On the right of the painting is a stove door through which the axe head can be placed to be heated and softened before being placed on an anvil and hammered to a sharp point. The platform in front of the miner is the anvil, on top of which a mallet has been placed. Hung Jui-Lin has depicted the interior space of the metal shop in detail using a charcoal. The maintenance equipment, the form of human figures in the painting, or the shape of the anvil for repairing metal objects have all been depicted, and then diluted color has been applied to express light and darkness. Entrenched in the details of the miners’s lives, Hung Jui-Lin refers to his paintings as the miners’ diary. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Repairing Tools on an Anvil

listRow.content: Huaishan Colliery was originally called Reifang First Pit. The management offices and dormitories were built of timber during the Japanese colonial period. The timber material and structure of the houses can be seen from the paintings. The 1950s was an era when  coalmines flourished, and the colliery required two shifts of workers. The house in the painting is lit brightly from the inside, while the exterior is cloaked in darkness. It is presumably the management office at dusk or nighttime. The artist is likely still at work when he depicted this image. The foreground is dark, especially under the eaves. The depiction of the brightly illuminated interior seen in the distance through the window is similar to the scenes inside the pit in the search for light within darkness, characteristic of Hung Jui-Lin’s works from this period. The figure seated inside, leaning against the window by the door has their back turned from the viewer, the figure on left is seen through the window to be reading a scroll. The human figures are not the focus for Hung Jui-Lin, but depicts his place of work, the management office with a tranquil sense of poetics. Expressing such a rustic and refined scene in the rigid, course colliery imparts Hung Jui-Lin’s uncommon abilities of observation and his internal clarity. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Office at Night

listRow.content: While waiting for the minecarts to bring them into the pit, the group of miners typically discuss important aspects or processes, or ways to overcome difficulties they may encounter in the workday. This is organized and announced by the foreman. There may be a tacit understanding within the group, but repeated communication improves efficiency. The group of miners depicted here have gather around in discussion. Hung Jui-Lin documents this scene as a bystander. A distracted miner on the left foreground turns to steal a glance at the artist at work, and the moment is instantly painted by Hong Jui-Lin.  The artist is able to capture an instant of dynamism in an otherwise static scene, which provides insight into Hung Jui-Lin’s ability to make detailed observations within time constraints that enables him to paint a momentary glance exchanged with a miner. Human forms can only be outlined in ink in this quick sketch group portrait in semi-darkness, but the postures and gestures of each figure preoccupied with their own thoughts are simply and vividly brought together. The minor gesture of the figure standing in profile at the center right, smoothing his shirt conveys a sense of authenticity in the characters, while the light wash of yellow applied in horizontal strokes on the front row of figures creates an atmosphere of warmth before the day breaks. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Exchanging Opinions

listRow.content: This painting depicts miners waiting in line for an administrative staff to tabulate their attendance records or registration information in order to settle their salaries. The verification process requires miners to be processed one at a time. The administrative staff bows his head in concentration as he carefully records information. He has a dip pen in his hand, and there is an open inkwell, bottle cap, and ledger on the desk. Because they need to be processed individually, the miners wait patiently. The administrative staff is clearly the focal point of the work, as his action differs from the others. Seated on his left is a figure who might have completed the process, appearing relaxed with a cigarette in hand, and turned toward the left. The remaining figures vary in their expressions. The figure standing behind the administrative staff is gazing down at what is being noted, the figure standing to his right is also looking at the ledger. On the far right, the figure gazes off toward the right of the painting as if distracted. The light in the painting comes from the above and ahead. Though the background has been rendered with diluted ink, a few brushstrokes suggest a window. Wages are being distributed in this office. Hung Jui-Lin has captured another facet in the life of the miner. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Payday

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin began working at the mines in 1938. In 1955 he eschewed realism and developed this silhouetted imagery of miners. With 17 years of experience and understanding of the operations at a coalmine, he was extremely familiar with miners’ actions and work scenarios. In the darkness of the pit, the miners’ headlamps are pointed forward and they appear as dark shadows, much like these black figures, to Hung Jui-Lin who observes them from behind; this is an effect created by the light source. Furthermore, the miners are black as ink from the coal dust, which might have inspired him to use silhouettes to express the contours of the mine workers. On the far right of this work, a miner stands inside a pit with a support prop (wooden post used for roof support). Two miners crouch in front, and one seated with a pickaxe is depicted hewing at the coal levels. The two standing figures on the left are maintenance workers making a wooden frame. A minecart in the distance is indicated below his hand with a miner crouched at the narrow entry waiting to progress. Elements combined in works such as this, of silhouettes or of a collage of symbols, vary with each work, but they enable the viewer to immediately sum up the nature and character of the miners in one glance. Using simplified symbols to represent human figures allows for a more expansive space for audience imagination. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Silhouette of Miners

title: A Quiet Time at the Office

listRow.content: An empty trolly and another filled with acacia logs, as well as a stretch of electrical wires on pylons and a small hut can be seen through the glass windows and open door of the administrative office. Within the small frame of this painting, the relationship between the interior and exterior has been extended further by the doorway and window in this ingenious choice of subject. The interior is deserted and silent. There is an abacus, ink well, dip pen, and notebook on the desk. A pickaxe has been laid on the ground beside the window. There are traces of human activity in the tranquil atmosphere. Concerned with the safety of mine workers, Hung Jui-Lin would often watch as miners descend into the mine pit. Perhaps the miners have already entered the pit, hence the office seems uncharacteristically quiet, allowing him to also feel a moment of quietude. Many objects remain in the dimly lit interior which create a chiaroscuro with the brightly light outdoor scenery. The light outside the window scatters on the open notebook on the desk, which appear especially bright along with the beads on the abacus. Through this tranquil composition Hung Jui-Lin amalgamates light, color, and perspective to create one of the few still-life paintings among Hung Jui-Lin’s works of the mining district. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: A Quiet Time at the Office

title: Three Miners
medium: Ink and pigment on cotton paper

listRow.content: The painting depicts three miners resting on a long bench by the window. Hung Jui-Lin outlines the silhouettes of the figures using an inked brush, and adds diluted ink to the shaded areas such as the neck, back, or shoulders, to nimbly reveal the dimensionality of the figures. The figure on the right sits cross-legged, resting with his head bowed and eyes closed. The man in the center is lost in thought with both arms extended and resting on the bench. The miner on the left is bare chested, with a hand on his chin. The speed of the brushwork can be seen whether in the lines of the figures or the backdrop. Hung Jui-Lin has a faithful grasp on the expressions and gestures of the figures before him. He omits superfluous color and uses leaving-blank (liubai) to create the miners’ clothing to set them apart from the background. The background has been created by first applying diluted rendered color, and then a creating the wooden frames of the window using a brush with diluted ink, replete with the interest of Eastern brush and ink painting. The precision of the quick sketch brushwork on the human figures is established on a solid foundation of drawing. The freehand calligraphic technique in the background are an ink wash expression. This work has been signed “礦山人 (Man from the Mountain Mines)” in Chinese, and “JL HUNG” in English. The overall brushwork in the painting is nimble, the color application pure, transparent and refined – exemplifying a meeting of Western and Eastern artistic techniques. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Three Miners

tfam.Media Technology: Ink and pigment on cotton paper

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin spent 35 years of his life underground, bearing witness to the perils in the life of miners. He said, “Mining work is a battle between life and death. I often feel a sense of anxiety in painting them, and this anxiety is reflected in my psyche. I don’t have time to ruminate on the elegance of lines, my sense of anxiety produces intense lines.” This work depicting miners seated in wait for the mine cart was painted in the pit illustrates the mood of anxiety that Hung Jui-Lin describes. The faces of the miners are blurred and unclear in the weak lighting, the outlines and application of color all convey speed and apprehension. This is the reality inside the pit. The miner standing and two of the miners seated on the right of the painting look intently at the artist. The three seated miners have their arms crossed on their thighs. They are confined in a small space without any daylight. Their faces blacked and their bodies exhausted, the miners have an indifferent, listless expression. Hong Jui-Lin expresses an aspect of the miners’ life of toil. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Waiting for the Mining Car

title: A Corner of the Metal Shop

listRow.content: This work depicts two teams of workers in the metal shop. The group on the right are quench-tempering a pickaxe; the second from the right is slightly hunched and focused on the anvil, making a hammering motion. The two on the left seem to be repairing corrective equipment. The second on the left is holding a hammer, while the first on the left is seems to be tightening the equipment. Using charcoal pencils, Hung Jui-Lin captured the vivid postures of these two groups of miners as they work on maintenance. He has omitted details of their faces, and only the two faces on the left can be seen. The others are concentrating on their own work, with their heads lowered or their backs to the artist. Hung Jui-Lin’s intention is to depict the dynamism in their work and the relationship between them, rather than present a portrait of a specific miner. The scene depicted is in the metal shop. Although we are not in the mine pit, the light seems muted and dimmed. He began by drawing the outlines of the human figures and equipment in charcoal, and then applied a brown watercolor. Hung Jui-Lin intends to express the collaboration between the characters, as well as another scene of professional dedication among the miners in the colliery, while revealing the interconnection between the many busy work arenas within the coalmine. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: A Corner of the Metal Shop

listRow.content: A miner, stove, furnace, and circular shapes on the wall in this 1953 painting depict a moment in the miners’ rest area. These four elements have been concisely depicted in precise, stable lines that tend toward symbolic representation. What captures the attention within the composition, is the bright and highly saturated stove. Behind the stove is the furnace that keeps the bento boxes warm, which is almost hidden in the background wall. The miner standing by the stove with his arms folded. The contour lines of the figure are thick, dark and strong, but the color blends into the wall. The bright ochre stove is bathed in light and becomes the brightest point of the composition. In the laborer’s dormitory, Hung Jui-Lin has painted several works of miners in a state of relaxation. These are usually of groups of miners chatting at ease. This work uses saturated, gloomy colors. Although there are patches of light on the body of the miner, he remains surrounded by darkness. The lack of details in the face and clothing make this work stylistically unique.  (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Warming by the Stove

listRow.content: The hoist depends on the power of the motor to pull cages filled with coal up to the mine entrance. The technicians who maintain the motorized hoists are not miners, and are responsible for mechanical repairs and maintenance. When machinery malfunction in the pit, they must also enter the pit to provide assistance. Although they are not engaged in coal production, they control the safety of the miners. The hoist technicians outside the pit have an established system of signals with the miners in the pit. For instance, one sound signals that the cage will stop, two sounds signal that the cage is ascending, three sounds indicate the cage is descending, four continuous sounds indicates that the cage is ascending at a speed. These subtle tasks cannot be taken lightly as they affect the safety of the miners. This painting depicts mechanics working in the machine room housing the motorized hoist as they observe whether the motor operating the hoist is functioning properly. In an era before the proliferation of cameras, Hung Jui-Lin’s adept sketching techniques distinctly depicted cable coils, bearings, chains, hooks, and cables so that viewers can see aspects of each aspect of the mining process. The motorized hoist of a height equal to an adult human, and the personnel who maintain it, are the soul of the work in the mines. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Examining a Hoist

listRow.content: When miners enter the slope to collect coal from the crosscut, powerful motorized hoists are required in order to pull the coal up to the surface. The angle of minecart tracks cannot exceed 23.5 degrees, or else the filled minecarts are likely to topple. If the angle is too small, the distance of the tracks would be excessively long and time consuming, hence, laying tracks required specialized design calculations. The motorized hoists necessitated regular maintenance with spare parts replaced regularly to ensure safety in the mine. This work, Examining a Hoist is a depiction of such a scenario. Three of the five mechanics have crouched down to inspect the cable coil bearing. One of the two workers standing is pulling on the crane; while the other stands in profile in the narrow space, off-balance with one leg bent and the other extended -- he braces himself against a pole for support as he tries to get a look at what the issue might be. Both are focused on contributing to the effort. In this sketch, Hung Jui-Lin fully applies his skillful depiction of the human body and composition of crowd scenes. The flowing brush and ink lines imbue the image with an immersive sense. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Operating a Hoist

listRow.content: Maintenance is the key to safety. The motorized hoist ferries several trolleys full of miners to work in the drifts in the pit. When they fill the trolleys with coal, the motor transports the full carts out of the mine. It must be carefully and consistently maintained to ensure safety, The cable spool in this image is quite large. It is located in the hoist room which has been established at a high elevation on a mountain and is frequently maintained. Rusty motorized hoists and machine rooms still remain today at the site of defunct mining factories; these motorized hoists have been abandoned in the mountains because they are too heavy to transport. In this work, two mechanics are crouched down, immersed in their maintenance work. The cable coil pictured belongs to a large-scale motorized hoist. There is a crane hook and chain above it. The contours have been drawn using a bamboo brush, and shading has been texturized with a dry brush, without filling in with color. In this skillful sketch using solely ink wash on paper, the artist has chosen a scene that would not otherwise been in public view. The mechanics under his brush are aware that these mechanical operations are crucial to safety, and that all must be maintained to proper order. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Repairing a Hoist Motor

listRow.content: A hoisting system is required to pull the trollies that transport coal from underground to the surface, or to ferry miners one to two thousand meters underground to work in the mine drifts. Powerful motors drive the transport in the main drift, motors with less horsepower are used in the mine drift of the slope road that transport to-and-from the main shaft. Motors also drive the ventilation systems. The shirtless miner in the painting is attempting to life a motor on his own, an indication that this motor is smaller than the one in the machine room housing the motorized hoist. Perhaps it is faulty and requires maintenance and so must be moved. Accidents and disasters are likely to occur if motors are improperly maintained. These four miners intend to carry the motor to the Metal Shop for repairs. Their faces are not depicted in detail in this work that mainly expresses a moment of collaboration between the four, and captures a scene where one of the men kneels in an attempt to hoist a yoke carrying the motor onto his own shoulders while three others are look on and stand in alert in order to step in to help when needed. The mutuality of this relationship and sentiment moved Hung Jui-Lin to depict it. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Workmen Lifting a Motor

listRow.content: This miner, Master Wen De sits quietly as Hung Jui-Lin’s model. His posture is relaxed, his gaze seems pensive, his broad shoulders and solid chest muscles have been fortified through hard labor. Hung Jui-Lin must have had ample time to sketch Master Wen De, as he was able to depict Master Wen De’s head, face, and body stance in careful detail. A soft natural light from above illuminates the miner’s face and chest, with a light shadow under the brim of the hat, the shoulders, and armpits. The work exudes an atmosphere of ease. The figure in the work is referred to as Master Wen De presumably because he has considerable mining experience, and is a senior miner whom Hung Jui-Lin trusts and relies upon. Hung Jui-Lin often reviewed and added to his sketches after returning home from his day at the mines. He would mumbling to himself “good miner, easy to talk to,” and then sheds tears when he added, “but ill-fated.” As a mine director, Hung Jui-Lin needed the assistance of a good foreman to manage affairs in order to ensure abundant production as well as guarantee the miners’ safety. At the same time, miners who were conscientious also toiled more than others. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Miner, Master Wen-te

title: Ten O'clock in the Morning at the Tamsui River

listRow.Title: Ten O'clock in the Morning at the Tamsui River

title: Miners Resting and Talking
medium: Ink and pigment on cotton paper

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin usually used ink wash to outline and paint miners. In this work, he used a dip pen and blue ink to depict a scene from the workmen’s hut. The thickness of the lines depicting the figures varies greatly. Occurrences of ink rendering can be seen where the pen begins, turns, or pauses; as well as in a few scattered ink specks. The wall has been brushed over with a broad brush and diluted ink. The table top has also been filled in with a few strokes of diluted ink. The light brown stripes on the left intend to suggest wooden window frames. Besides their contours, the figures have been left blank without color, using surface color to offset the contour lines of the figures. This media and painting technique is rarely seen. Eight miners sit around a large rectangular table in the painting, there is a pickaxe on the table, and a blue water bottle that becomes a focal point. There are also wrapped lunch boxes. The miner next to the stove with his legs crossed is the visual center; the slightly hunched Uncle Ah-tien behind him looks on. Everyone is waiting at the workmen’s hut for the workday to begin. This workmen’s hut is located next to the entrance to the pit. Hung Jui-Lin has completed a number of works from various angles set in this workmen’s hut. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Miners Resting and Talking

tfam.Media Technology: Ink and pigment on cotton paper

listRow.content: The scene in this work resembles that of the work Miners Getting Warm, but they were completed in 1952 and 1949 respectively. The figures and positions in the two works are quite similar; a notable difference is in the pencil outlines seen in the 1949 painting, which is absent in this painting – seemingly painted directly with a bamboo brush. There is a small coal burner for heating water or warming lunches behind the main stove in Miners Getting Warm. Working in the rainy autumn and winter seasons of Ruifang, miners usually gather around the stove for warmth and for conversation, sharing information about the various mine shafts as well as mining tips. Using nimble lines, Hung Jui-Lin has painted the miners’ moment of relaxation centered around the stove. The work does not appeal with arduous labor or surrender, or express using gloomy hues, but depicts the solid, honest faces of each miner with simple precision. Hung Jui-Lin has positioned himself directly across from the stove, so the figures become gradually smaller from the left foreground to the center due to perspective. The spatial relationship between the miners in the foreground and background have been adroitly handled. His paintings of miners in the early 1950s were varied and rich in themes. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Chatting by the Stove

listRow.content: In his Ode to Miners, Hung Jui-Lin had this description of miners. “You are cloaked with being obtuse, unrefined, ugly, drunken, impoverished, gamblers; but your true essence is grit, adventurous, brave, modest, candor, serene.” The expressions and posture of the miners in his work all exemplify modesty and candor. In this rather unique perspective and composition, the facial features and body contours of the two figures in the foreground are relatively distinct and complete, while the four figures in the back appear blurred and obscured by distance. Everyone is fully dressed, and there is a burgeoning sense of commotion in the stillness, perhaps an anxious anticipation, or a silence while waiting for dispatch. The six figures do not share a uniform direction of gaze, each is immersed in their own thoughts with a touch of resignation. They are illuminated from the right side of the painting, which oscillates on the obscured faces and silhouettes. The disparate gazing direction among the six figures creates a dramatic tension. This depiction of an ordinary scene at the mines is a refined work of miners. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Miners-Group Portrait

listRow.content: There are two carts in the foreground of this work, one that is empty, and another that is ferrying five laborers. They have likely just finished dumping waste rock on top of the mound of rock spoil and are riding the cart back down the waste pile. The cart gathers speed as it slides down the hill. One man is seated at the front of the cart, and the other three stand along the hoarding of the cart. They each casually occupy a corner of the cart. Another man stands on a wooden plank outside of the cart. Actually, this is against regulation and dangerous, but the miners have decided to ride the cart for convenience. A  workmen’s hut can be seen in the distance, and a mountain range in the far distance, showcasing the geography and scenery of the mining communities of Northern Taiwan. Hung Jui-Lin once said that he would look around and paint on days when work was light at the mines, and was well received by the Ni family. In this lighthearted work, he captures a moment when the rough and guileless miners return to the mines. He first used pencil to outline and arrange the composition, with a focus on the figures in the cart. Diluted color has then been rendered over the entire work, which he described as a form of keeping a mining diary. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: The Workday is Over

listRow.content: The errand runner at the mines does not enter into the pit. This figure is likely an errand runner judging from the fact that he is not shirtless, nor does he have a headlamp on his hat. He has a youthful visage, but lacks youthful vitality, with a sense of sadness. Hung Jui-Lin has outlined the silhouette of the figure using ink, and then brushed over the hat, face, and clothing using a broad brush and brown tones. The shaded areas of the face have been indicated using maroon on the side of the nose and under the eyes. This color work that includes gloomy tones of brown, tan, ochre, and grey-blue may seem capricious but in actuality establishes the basic colors for the paintings of miners, and differs in atmosphere from other character sketches done in pencil and ink. The artist perhaps added to the colors and filled in lines after a quick on-the-spot sketch. Heavier lines have been applied to the outlines of the figure’s shoulders and back of the neck in order to create a distance with the background. Extra lines have also been applied on the clothing to indicate folds and shadows in the fabric. There is a vague shape in the background that suggests a passage into the mine pit. Hung Jui-Lin’s paintings and drawings were always intuitive. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Workman, Ah-tu

listRow.content:
This work depicts miners resting and chatting in the coal yard of the Huaishan Colliery. The yard is located at two-stories above ground level. A mountain seen in the distance to the south is Sanzhuazi Mountain, and Sandiaoling Mountain can be seen to the east. The direction from which the mountain is seen cannot be determined from the painting.

Seven mine workers are seated at random on an acacia logs. Their mutual gaze reveals a relationship of interaction. Bamboo scoops and pickaxes used by mine workers are scattered on the ground. The emerald green of the mountain range offsets the white shirts on the miners, seemingly expressing a relaxing aspect of the colliery on a summer day.  The artist has used pencil to sketch first, and then added watercolors in a freehand style. Paintings of mineworkers using watercolors were rarely seen in 1951. Hung Jui-Lin is not particular about painting tools or media. It was in this frame of mind during a moment of respite that he created these authentic works depicting the daily lives of miners. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Miners Chatting

listRow.content:
This work is an upward view of the rock spoil heap at the Huaishan Coalmine. At the far right is a pit entrance, and the path on the left goes up along the path the top of the rock spoil heap. Miners dump waste rocks and soil here, which has accumulated over time into a barren dirt hill. The rock spoil heap is a pile built of accumulated spoil – the waste rock and soil removed during the excavation of drifts or in the process of mining coal. These are transported in carts to the top of the hill and dumped into the valley. Over time, this accumulates into a mound or dirt heap. 

Rock spoil mounds are not solid rock, but are loose structures that can wash away in heavy rain and cause mudslides. This is the spoil slope depicted in the foreground. In the distance are two verdant mountain peaks, possibly the Sandiaoling Mountain. The rock spoil mound for Huaishan Colliery (now the Longdu Mountain in Ruifang) had an elevation of around 200 meters. This work is imbued with the characteristics of the coalmine. Hung Jui-Lin has integrated the arduous life of the miners into the familiar landscape.  (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Spoil Tip

title: Miss B
medium: Janpanese 4x5 film negative on bromide paper with hand-tinting

tfam.Media Technology: Janpanese 4x5 film negative on bromide paper with hand-tinting

listRow.content: In Resting Spoil Tip Workers, there are four figures wearing bamboo hats and in bare feet. From their skirts and appearance, they are presumably female errand runners. There is a large water kettle on the table with drinking water for everyone. They have a calm expression as they await work assignments. Prior to 1960, there were dozens of female miners at the Reisan Coalmine, but this was prohibited by government decree in 1964 and only men were allowed to work in the mines. The women in this work were likely responsible for work outside of the mines. In addition to helping with dumping waste rocks and soil on the rock spoil mound, they can also help sort coal, or collect coal remnants at the rock spoil mound to supplement the family’s income. Even though they were paid half of what the male miners made, they persisted despite the hardship. After the women miners finished their workday, the returned home and tended to housework. They contributed equally and deserve compassion. This brushwork in this painting was accelerated. Lines were first laid to sketch out the space between the figures, furniture, and the overall space within the hut, then diluted ink and saturated ink were rendered and texturized, using ink traces and leaving blank to express light. The brushstrokes created by the bamboo brush crystalized a moment of sentiment. This is characteristic of Hung Jui-Lin’s style. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Resting Spoil Tip Workers

title: Picking up Coal by the River

listRow.content: The women and children of the mining communities, rather than the miners, feature as subjects of this work. They are busy, bent over and preoccupied with picking for coal among the mound of rock spoil. The mound in the distance is the mound of rock spoil for the Huaishan Coalmine where coalminers can be seen pushing a cart of waste rocks and soil that will be discarded. Often, the waste soil and rocks contain remnants of coal, so the women and children would pick through this in search of coal which they collect in their bamboo scoops. They use small hammers to tap on the remnants to separate the coal from stones. The larger remnants they find can be sold, and the smaller remnants could be used at home – both help supplement the household income. Women and children worked hard at finding remnant coal. This was a part of life in the coal districts during that time, which also illustrated the economic hardships among the miners’ families. In this quick sketch, Hung Jui-Lin has arranged a group of figures in various positions. The figures and their actions enable us to understand at a glance that they are foraging for remnant coal. Regardless of whether they are women wearing a bamboo hat, or children with towels on their heads, all of their faces are concealed but for one woman in white. She gazes back at the artist, and expresses the artist’s humanity. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Picking up Coal by the River

listRow.content: This work and View of Metal Shop depict the same scene, but from a slightly different angle. However, the works are dated a year a part. This work was completed in 1951, while View of Metal Shop was dated 1950. This timber house from the Japanese-era is where the motors and machinery are repaired. The structure of the columns and beams are a main focus of the composition. The complex objects of motors and miscellaneous machinery awaiting repair combined with the miner at work create a scene of tranquil harmony. The interior itself is dark, but appears especially warm with an angled beam of sunlight. This appears to be a quiet afternoon. The miscellaneous objects in the foreground and the space behind the wooden columns and beams are orderly, the wealth of information conveyed by the setting and the movement of the figure and objects highlight Hung Jui-Lin’s abilities to manage spatial perspectives and light. Using transparent watercolors and the rendering of ink wash within a unified tone, he has depicted another atmosphere found in the colliery. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Interior of Metal Shop

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin painted several works depicting miners warming themselves in the workmen’s hut. In this work, two miners, one seated and the other standing, wait in the stove-heated hut for work to begin. They are both dressed in long-sleeved shirts and long trousers indicating that the weather had turned cold. The blue-shirted miner stands slightly cowering next to the stove with his arms resting on his abdomen, as though hoping the stove would warm his body as quickly as possible. The seated miner is resting with his legs crossed and eyes closed, as though he is enjoying a rare moment of respite. The stove burns coal, and has a long stove pipe, the coal grate at the bottom has not been latched, and some ash remains to be cleared. Inside the timber house, mountains can be seen at a distance through the window panes. A shovel and sundry items have been placed under the window. Comparable to documentary photography, daily life at the mines is realistically depicted under Hung Jui-Lin’s brush, but these paintings additionally convey the humanistic concern of this participant observer. Hung Jui-Lin describes his paintings as a diary of the miners. With his pens, he bore witness to their lives for over three decades, and had come to realize that the same philosophy governs that which is beautiful or ugly. Real life is the concept that these works depicting miners seek to convey. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Warming by a Stove

title: Uncle Ah-tien and His Miner Friends

listRow.content: This work depicts miners resting in a workmen’s hut equipped with a stove, which is partially shown in the lower left corner. On the whole, the work captures a rarely seen scene of warmth in the mines. Standing on the left is the loyal and reliable Uncle Ah-tien, who often appears in Hung Jui-Lin works. He is distinctively dressed in a traditional Minnan open-collar shirt with short and wearing a brimless cap -- a style typical among elderly men in Taiwan. He has a pen in his right hand, and holds his left hand behind his back, as though he had been writing something. Uncle Ah-tien’s role is to maintain the minecarts, to grease the cart wheels and ensure they run smoothly. Three miners are seated. The miner in the middle touchingly holds his child who has fallen asleep on his lap. Children in the mining communities sometimes come to the mines to wait for their fathers at the end of the workday, and would play with other children from the mining community. Perhaps exhausted from playing, the child in the picture has dozed off on his father’s lap. Hung Jui-Lin had a kind and humble disposition. This warm scene inspired him to depict an aspect of the miners as they enjoying the happiness of family. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Uncle Ah-tien and His Miner Friends

listRow.content:
Hung Jui-Lin’s relationship with the miners comes from a place of respect and concern. Spending time with them from dawn till dusk each day, he naturally had an understanding of their individual temperaments and family situations. Many miners had spouses, parents, or children working in the same mine. Hung Jui-Lin’s father-in-law was formerly his manager at the mine; he was not only familiar with the work environment at the mines, but also imparted many suggestions to Hung Jui-Lin on managing the mines. 

The sincerity and concern Hung had toward the miners in turn inspired their dedication and hard work, as well as their willingness to pose for his drawings. The miner Ah-hsi depicted here is a relative of Hung Jui-Lin’s. According to Chin S. Houng, Ah-hsi was aware of the dangers of working in the mines, and later changed professions to become a rickshaw driver who ferried passengers from the Ruifang Train Station. This portrait of Ah-hsi is depicted from a slightly downward angle. The figure’s brows are furrowed as he gazes forward. His lips are slightly parted. He seems to have been quite a personality with his prominent nose, tussled hair, and goatee. The light falls on his face from his right, and is clearly demarcated from the shadowed side of his face by the bridge of his nose. The background of diluted ink on the left brings the figure to the fore. Everything is expressed with the brush and ink. Hung Jui-Lin’s talent and his early endeavors in sketching have culminated in his ability to capture an aura in an instant. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Miner, Ah-hsi

title: Half-Length Portrait of a Young Miner

listRow.content:
Front:
Miners work in a hazardous and arduous environment with a high rate of attrition. Some laborers leave after collecting their wages for a day of work or two. This painting depicts a newly recruited mine worker with a shy expression. He stands erect and reserved in profile, with his hands clasped together. The background was created using a thick brush saturated with ink, which contrasts against the figure drawn using diluted ink and leaving-blank (liubai). The viewer can sense his anxiety and cautiousness. Hung Jui-Lin uses thick black lines heavy with ink to outline the contours from the top of the figure’s head and around to the shoulders and his back, highlighting his physique as well as creating a focal effect similar to using a close-up lens on a camera. Judging from the delicate rendering of the brushwork and ink color, and the manipulation of the wet brush, this work must have been completed within a short time frame. For Hung Jui-Lin, who graduated from the Western Art Department of the Tokyo Imperial Art School (Bijutsu Gakkō) during the 50s when oil painting materials were difficult to come by, painting with the brush, ink, and rice paper left by his father seemed especially suited to depicting mine workers in the colliery. 

Back: 
Entering from the pit entrance to the mine drift required passing through the main mine shaft, then entering the branching drifts. The mine shafts could be over 1000 meters from the mine entrance, so minecarts were used to bring miners in and out of the mine pit. This work depicts three linked carts. Usually, each cart would ferry four to six people. The image shows some people still standing. As the height in the mine drift gradually decreased, they would have to sit down when the cart entered the pit. The miners who were responsible for the winding engine upon entering the pit would use a whistle to warn when the cart would move forward or retreat. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Half-Length Portrait of a Young Miner

listRow.content: The basic equipment for miners entering the mine includes the canvas hat, headlamp, batteries, first-aid kit, lunch sack, water flask, pickaxe, and saw, etc. This miner is shirtless with clothing draped over his shoulders and in his right hand, which also carries his lunch sack. Interestingly, he does not hold a pickaxe in his right hand, but a wooden rod of his same height. Hung Jui-Lin has outlined the miner’s contours in ink, and then applied diluted color. There is a shirt tied around his shoulders as well as a brown towel. The clothing in his hands look clean, which indicates that his is preparing to enter the mine. Senior miner Chou Chao-nan explains that the miner is holding an acacia wood support prop needed inside the pit. Wood of varying length and girth are needed for construction in the mine drifts. This miner must have selected a required length of wood before entering the mine. His expression seems more relaxed than that of someone entering the mine, so he may have chosen a rod and is preparing to go home. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Going Home after Work

listRow.content: Around 1950, Hung Jui-Lin often sketched individual portraits of the miners he knew well, and was concerned for. Among the most memorable of his subjects was Uncle Ah Kuenzai because Hung Jui-Lin had presented then-president Mr. Chiang Ching-kuo with a portrait of Uncle Ah-kun when the president visited Hung Jui-Lin’s “35 Years of Mine Workers Forms” exhibition in 1979. In the portrait, Uncle Ah-kun is not wearing his headlamp and canvas hat. He is in a shirt and shorts, perhaps resting and in a daze after work. Hung Jui-Lin outlined the figure using diluted ink, and then uses diluted ink and dry ink to rub in light and shadows, using intentional blank spaces (liubai) for the brightest areas. The work gives the impression of a pencil drawing. Uncle Ah-kun was symbolic of the hardworking, rugged miner who was diligent and does not complain. With deep lines on his forehead, sunken cheeks, and furrowed brows, he sits on the ground wearing slippers he made from pieces of rubber he has cut for himself. This crude simplicity is precisely the nature of the miner. Hung Jui-Lin was devoted to depicting his profound observations of their harsh lives. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Portrait of Uncle Ah-kun

listRow.content: The pickaxe is the miner’s most intimate tool of the trade. It is a T-shaped hand tool with a metal head mounted perpendicularly on a wooden handle. The head may have a pointed end on one side and a flat end on the other, or two pointed ends. It is indispensable whether for coal or mineral mining. After work, miners would squat on the ground, sharpening the edges of their pickaxes. This particular miner has a gaunt face, and his back is hunched. This was often the result of long-term overwork and alcoholism. He carries his pickaxe over his right shoulder, and carries his lunch bag in his lefthand. With a weathered face and blank stare, he accepts this work as his fate. Using a moistened, saturated solid line Hung Jui-Lin outlines the left side of the miner’s silhouette, which is the side closer to the viewer. The pickaxe and clothing on his right, and the lunch bag are painted using a relatively dry brush, creating a perspective effect of distance, where the virtual and real coexist. There is a look of exhaustion and weariness to the miner; and his hat, hair, and facial features have been rendered with a skillful brush, thanks to Hung Jui-Lin’s adroit brushwork. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Miner Carrying a Pickaxe

listRow.content: This young, gentle miner has an air of inexperience, and may be a new employee. There was a high attrition rate for mine workers. It was a job that required high-levels of physical strength which an average person could not endure. This miner has not experienced hardships, his muscles have not been deformed by drudgery. His eyes still glimmer with youthful understanding. He is wearing a soft canvas hat with a headlamp, and is shirtless and in shorts, revealing his strong arms. A towel is draped around his neck. This is the usual dress of miners at the time. Aluminum hats had not yet been produced in the early 50s, and were not prevalent until 1969. After taking time to observe, Hung Jui-Lin made the sketch quickly. He focused most of his efforts on the miner’s face, followed by his body shape and posture. Hung Jui-Lin was not emphasizing anything in particular because the miner did not have a particular message to convey. Hung Jui-Lin earnestly painted their frankness and simplicity which produced an aesthetic clarity. The viewer can sense the strength in the body of this laborer and his attitude of sincerity. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Young Miner

title: Mine Maintenance Worker Holding a Saw

listRow.content: In 1951, Hung Jui-Lin sketched a number of seated portraits of miners, as well as painted their portraits using brush and ink. During this period, he had not yet begun bringing simple art materials into the mine pit to depict group scenes. Mine workers’ roles are not limited to collecting coal. They may also work as drillers, timberers, or hewers. The drillers bore holes for placing explosives to expose the coal surface for picking. The hurrier transported filled carts from the mine to the surface. The timberer fashioned and installed timber supports to prop up the walls and ceiling of the mine shaft to prevent cave-ins. The hewers who hewed the coal with a pickaxe might also install timber props in the drifts, and might also need to use a saw. The miner depicted here by Hung Jui-Lin rests his right hand on the wooden handle of his pickaxe between his legs. According to regulation, support props must be installed no more than a meter apart. Miners must dodge these props when they collect coal in small spaces. The figure depicted holds a saw in his hands, and not a pickaxe. He is wearing Japanese era waraji sandals woven from straw. Although shoes made from rubber and plastic were available in the 1950s, many miners could not afford them and were barefooted. They developed thick callouses on their feet over time. This work is a document that preserves the image of miners of that era. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Mine Maintenance Worker Holding a Saw

listRow.content: Impoverished, arduous, and fraught with danger: why would anyone choose the life of a miner? Most mine workers were born to lives of poverty with no other option. There were few factory jobs available in the agrarian society. And the harvest was not always sufficient even for those with some land to farm, compelling them to take on higher paying work. Miners would often say, “I may die by working in the mines, but the whole family will perish if I don’t work in the mines.” By working, miners may die from mining accidents, but if they don’t work to supplement the household income, their families may starve. The miners seem resigned to this life as a result of this spirit of self-sacrifice. Their work often requires long periods of waiting – waiting to enter or exit the mine, waiting to collect their wages. These are the moments that provided opportunities for Hung Jui-Lin to make sketches. In this work, the young miner depicted in profile appears expressionless. His blank stare seems to be an expression common to miners when they are wait around. This work was completed in 1951, when miners still wore canvas hats with headlamps. This miner has rolled up his pantlegs and sits cross-legged. His hands rest on his knee and calf. The depiction of the joints in his curved fingers and is particularly detailed, while the textured folds of his sleeves are expressed in the light and shadows. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Portrait of Sitting Miner

title: Uncle Ah-kun on a Mining Car

listRow.content: Uncle Ah-kun was Hung Jui-Lin’s most frequent subject. He was in charge of moving the coal and waste rocks on minecarts outside the mines. Whether in the sweltering summer sun or when soaked in winter rain, he rarely utters even a word of complaint but is faithfully devoted to his job. Hung Jui-Lin regarded him as an exemplary miner, and has described how Uncle Ah-kun could sleep standing up when exhausted at work. He stayed at the mine throughout the year, and only washed up to go home for Chinese New Year when Hung Jui-Lin urged him to reunite with his family. In this work, Uncle Ah-kun sits next to a minecart that he dispatched. Using a single pencil line, Hung Jui-Lin sketched Ah Kun and the minecart in realistic detail. The cart is constructed of thick wooden planks that have been secured using metal sheets nailed to the corners. Hung Jui-Lin simplified a complex image by integrating the cart with the miner – a quintessential representation of the mine. Ah Kun’s hat and face have also been depicted in exquisite detail. He is drawn wearing handmade rubber sandals, and sitting with legs crossed; his overlapping hands rest on a knee. Hung Jui-Lin was able to preserve these silhouettes representative of miners by silently and carefully sketching. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Uncle Ah-kun on a Mining Car

title: Assistant Mine Director Reading an Announcement

listRow.content: For Hung Jui-Lin, art was present in daily life; it wasn’t necessary to seek art externally. Each moment, each scene of each day can be recorded. He regarded the mines as his studio where every event, object, and person encountered was a subject for his creativity. This assistant mine director visited the office, and is examining the day’s work schedule and time table. Hung Jui-Lin captured the scene by recording this unintentional gesture using the simplest lines. The assistant director’s brows, eyes, nose, lips and chin have been completed in a single continuous pencil line. Lights and shadows are not expressed in the simple lines, but they showcase a mastery of form and expression of temperament. The intent of his gaze, his mouth slightly agape, his rounded back and bald head are all expressed fittingly. The arm of his eyeglasses hooked over his ear point toward a bulletin board that contains a single notice, on which Hung Jui-Lin has signed, dated, and applied his seal, expressing the artist’s sense of humor. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Assistant Mine Director Reading an Announcement

title: Dumping Debris on the Spoil Tip

listRow.content:
This work created in 1950 is one of Hung Jui-Lin’s early works of miners, before he developed his characteristic ink and watercolor depictions of miners. Using pencil and watercolor, Hung Jui-Lin depicts five mine workers working together to dispose of a cart full of dirt and stones, guided by the miner at the center of the painting who is bent at the waist. He wants to open the side panel of the cart so that the dirt and stones can fall out. This figure, bent over to open the side panel is the most dynamic; the remaining four characters each have a unique pose, but are static. The figure in white on the right helps to prop up the cart, while the shirtless figure on the left is intently observing the figure bent over in exertion to lend a hand when needed. They are all attentive to the fellow at work. 
Each day, Hung Jui-Lin created profiles of the workers around him. He noticed every detail of their hardship and work. The miners are devoted to their work in order to carry the burden of supporting their families. They did not have extravagant wishes. This was a quality that Hung Jui-Lin found reverent and moving. This work of mine workers has a strong narrative sense. From the painting, we are able to easily read the message Hung Jui-Lin wishes to convey. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Dumping Debris on the Spoil Tip

listRow.content:
Uncle Ah-kun, who appears more frequently than any other in Hung Jui-Lin’s work, is tasked with leading the group of porters who bring waste materials to be emptied atop the rock spoil heap. The porters spend their days outside of the pit. They takeover when the minecarts exit the pit, and bring the coal to the storage yard, or else bring the carts full of waste rocks to the rock spoil heap. At the entrance to the pit, he must adjust the rail switch so that the minecarts can go where they need to go.
The cart rails are in the foreground, and a row of empty carts are lined up in the open area at the ready. Shirtless miners wearing headlamps are seated on an acacia log, chatting as they wait. On the far right there is a building. This scene is perhaps at the colliery. Judging from the shape of the distant mountains and the wires on the pylon, this depicts Reifang Colliery in 1950. In these seemingly carefree rapid sketches, Hung Jui-Lin could not have foreseen that each brushstroke would become valuable testaments to the Huaishan Colliery. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Resting beside a Spoil Car

listRow.content:
In the foreground of this work are minecart tracks winding through the colliery, as well as two overturned carts with their wheels showing, indicating that the cart wheels require changing or repair. This is a daily scene as well as the work of Uncle Akun. In the midground are three carts with several miners aboard. There is also a miner seated on the ground, and another standing. A chain of mountain peaks can be seen in the distance. This is a scene from Huaishan Colliery in 1950, when few miners were present, unlike the series of group portraits of miners painted after 1957, which features large groups of miners. 

Looking toward the distance from the Huaishan Colliery (present-day Reifang Park basketball court) is the Sanzhuazi Mountain in the distance. The colliery is the best location from which Hung Jui-Lin painted daily.

The artist began with a quick sketch in pencil, and then, applied large renderings of watercolor on the paper. The scene depicted appears breezy and light. The arrangement from near to far, from large to small, expresses perspective. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: View of Mine

listRow.content:
In both the harsh heat of summer and the frigid winds of winter, mineworkers who work outside the pit are tasked with pushing cartloads of dirt and rocks to the top of the mound of rock spoil to empty it. In this work, three shirtless laborers wearing bamboo hats are performing this labor-intensive manual work. The figure on the left wears a scarf intended to shield from the sun, and all three are barefooted as they work together to overturn the trolly. It can be seen that mine workers in the 1950s rarely wore shoes. Their footwear may be made of straw or homemade simple shoes. Although porters are not required to enter the pit, their level of exertion is equal to their colleagues in the pit. 

Colliery Number 2 at Reifang was located where the basketball court of present-day Reifang Park is situated. Judging from the expansive panorama of the work with the blue skies, white clouds, and green mountains in the distance, this work was likely painted from a perspective above the rock spoil heap at the colliery. According to Hung Jui-Lin’s nephew, who grew up in the Huaishan Colliery, the spoilage heap was near Longtan Mountain, elevation 199 meters. In the distance is Sanchaling Mountain. The work is expressed through highly saturated watercolor which is notably different in the style of expression in ink of the miner workers working in the depths of the mine pits. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Dumping Spoil Together

title: Sketch of Miners
medium: Ink and charcoal on cotton paper

listRow.content: The quick sketch group portrait of miners completed in 1950 uses thick black hard pencil lines to accurately and concisely depict the staggered positions of the five seated miners. He must have contemplated the position and order within. The facial features of the characters are merely suggested using lines, or even omitted. The proportions and postures of the human bodies have been perfectly grasped; the background is a large swath of diluted ink. The simple ink hues suggest distant mountains, and diluted ink on the ground beneath the figures indicates shadows, creating space and distance. Hung Jui-Lin’s long-term observation of the miners, distilling their forms almost into symbolic forms. This foreshadowed his entre into the group portraits of miners. After all, the miners he observes are often in groups, gathered together to rest, wait, talk. The lines of this work are crisp and clear. The sforms of the miners are expressed using simple lines. As he puts it, the figures he depicts are a “grasp of the body,” that is, grasping the lines of the subject. This is the most fundamental of painting skills. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Sketch of Miners

tfam.Media Technology: Ink and charcoal on cotton paper

listRow.content:
Front:
The miner and minecart are the most vivid representations of the mine. In this work, there are two miners and two empty minecarts. A miner sits on an overturned cart that is awaiting repair, while another miner in profile passes in front of Hung Jui-Lin, unaware that he is painting. This natural, undeliberate composition fully showcases Hung Jui-Lin’s creative state. His creativity, his work, and his life is completely integrated. Hung Jui-Lin once wrote, “Labor has become an emotive phrase over time. Actually, the life of a laborer is difficult for outsiders to truly understand. Without firsthand experience, one cannot comprehend this trial by fire, nor understand the amount of pain they endure.” He believed what he could accomplish from the perspective of a participant observer was to use the purest of brushstrokes to depict, stroke by stroke, their solid yet exhausted torsos; and to praise their sincerity, diligence, and professionalism. The pure lines and simple color application reveals a most rustic and unpretentious expression. 



Back:
Two miners have laid down in the mine to rest and chat. Their bodies are at ease and relaxed. The posture of two people reposed increases the complexity of the composition and perspective, but this is not unsurmountable for Hung Jui-Lin. The breadth of Hung Jui-Lin’s creative materials is also inadvertently revealed. Both the front and the back depicts two miners, using only outlines without further rendering but full of tension. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Miners and Mining Car

listRow.content: A “miner” is a generalized term for those who work in the mines, but these roles can be categorized into dozens of specializations. This work depicts the mechanical maintenance room at the mines, colloquially referred to as the “metal shop.” Hung Jui-Lin has created several works from different angles set in this Japanese-era timber house. In this particular work, Hung Jui-Lin is located directly opposite as he frames the scene, calmly and carefully sketching without disturbing the miners. Throughout the 1950s, Hung Jui-Lin painted every work area of the mine. We imagine him visiting every part of the process to observe and learn, hence some of his work depicting scenes outside the pit have been preserved. This painting depicts two mechanics with a minecart containing a motor. A pully is suspended from the ceiling. The two are likely repairing a motor. There is a stove on the left. The artist precisely presents the spatial layers of foreground, midground, and background in this interior, with an excellent grasp on the atmospheric expression of a complex space. Few of these works depicting work at the mines using watercolor and ink are seen after 1955, perhaps due to changes in his role in the mines. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: View of Metal Shop

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin said “The frank and unaffected expressions of miners correspond to my own spirit, and compel me at every moment to capture them with my paint brush.” As for this mute porter, Hung Jui-Lin does not disregard him because of his disability, but is more attentive to him, preserving his guileless, youthful appearance. The clear contrasts between light and shadow in this quick sketch is apparent in the intentional blank spaces (liubai) in the hat, cheek, and neck which clearly indicate the strong light illuminating from the right. Hung Jui-Lin outlines the contours of his form with bamboo brush using an ostensibly extemporaneous flowing freehand which, in fact, showcases several instances of flying-white (kasuri) technique, indicating his mastery of ink pigmentation and water content in his whimsical brushwork. Compared with pencil or charcoal works, ink wash expresses degrees of white, grey, and black, and is more able to convey the warm temperament in the characters and the supple textures in their clothing or skin. The textures of the brows and hair using the split-brush technique is remarkably dexterous. The irises of the eyes, rendered in saturated ink with an intentional blank space (liubai), are especially spirited. Not only is this a vivid portrait, but the beauty of ink wash is profoundly conveyed. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Mute Miner

listRow.content: This cross-legged miner is unusually dressed in a suit jacket, with his pantlegs rolled up and wearing a hat with a headlamp. Miners might dress arrive to work in Western-style suits during the winter to stave off the cold. This was perhaps the only suit the miner owned. This individual’s name isあきなみ (Akinami). He had a limp due to an injury caused during a collapse in the mines. His mother also worked in the colliery, and was an ill-fated woman. Hung Jui-Lin included many details in this portrait. After outlining the figure, hat, towel, and suit jacket and applying a light wash, he used a dry brush flying-white (kasuri) technique with bamboo brush over the figure. In the background to the right of the figure, he used wet ink to create an area of ink which highlights the figure. The figure is not illuminated on the left, and the shaded areas of his left cheek, shoulder, and the suit have all been expressed using ink wash. The figure is gazing directly at the artist Hung Jui-Lin, he is in a relaxed mood, with a slight smile. Though his eyes are veiled by the hat’s rim, a glimmer can be perceived. This cross-legged miner has set aside some free time to allow Hung Jui-Lin to sketch him, indicating a degree of familiarity with the artist. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Miner with Crossed Legs

listRow.content: This half-length portrait of miner Huo Wang emphasizes the figure’s jutting jaw using a bamboo brush without a preliminary pencil outline. His sunken cheeks have been accurately suggested with a single line. The forehead and right cheek have been illuminated. The miner’s wordless expression is conveyed through his furrowed brows, the level and steady gaze of the eyes, and his tightly pursed lips. His off-kilter hat has been depicted using lines of uneven weight where thick lines indicate shadows, and diluted colors set the illuminated areas apart. A dimensional effect is created using only a minimum of brushstrokes. His body and the towel around his neck have been formed with a few brushstrokes; color has not been applied so as to keep the focus on the face. Miners work under constant tacit pressure. They confronted the possibility of death on a daily basis and were not in control of their own fate. Hung Jui-Lin had empathy for their plight. They didn’t seem to harbor a sense of hope, but were focused solely on their work and survival. Miners were sometimes embroiled in altercations borne of frustration, but Hung Jui-Lin was profoundly moved by their kind nature, industrious attitude, and pure heart. He believed the essence of his art was in the pursuit of “authenticity,” and that miners were able to express human nature with authenticity, so he was drawn to paint them. The painting of this miner portrayed an authentic innocence. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Miner, Huo- wang

title: Miner Prepared to Enter the Mine

listRow.content:
This miner has been presented in a full-length portrait, with his torso disproportionally longer than his lower body -- indicating that Hung Jui-Lin’s view is from an angle above and in close proximity. The figure is shirtless without coal dust on his torso. He holds a bundle of clothing on his left and looks as though he is about to enter the pit, perhaps re-dressing after he washes up at the end of the day. 

Hung Jui-Lin uses a rigid pencil to draw the miner’s face, with a line on the broad right shoulder to suggest a collar bone. The pectorals, rib cage, and slightly sunken abdomen have been sketched with several strokes; the arms are lean, the legs are relaxed but powerful. This is a simple and concise depiction of the human body. Light washes of color have been applied onto the rigid pen lines, imbuing the painting with a rich variation of light and shadow. The miner’s shadow has been especially emphasized using both a rigid pen and soft brush which explores possibilities for integrating lines and color wash. The background of dark green provides a depth that highlights the pale-yellow tone of the human body; the headlamp radiates a directional yellow light that is rich in dramatic effect. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

listRow.content: Autumn and winter in the colliery of Ruifang was often overcast and raining, with low temperatures. The external environment felt especially cold by contrast when exiting from the high temperatures inside the mines. The workmen’s hut was equipped with a stove for the miners to keep warm. Captured by Hung Jui-Lin who was among them, this work depicts a group of miners chatting as they warm themselves around the stove. The stove serves as a boundary in the picture, with two people to its right and five to its left, each facing in a different direction and each with a unique posture, expression, and clothing. The figures overlap and the stove, slightly right of center, takes shape using only a few simple lines. Hung Jui-Lin outlined the entire drawing using pencil before strengthening the composition with brush and ink. The background has been rendered using a large brush with light pigmentation to construct a circular space with a sense of depth. With a limited amount of time to complete the work, Hung relied on simple, confident lines to capture the shape of these figures and the spatial relationships between them. The viewer is captivated by this light sketch of human expressions and movements, as though able to engage in conversation with the figures. This work showcases Hung Jui-Lin’s much lauded sketching abilities. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin used drawings rather than words to document his miner friends. He contemplated the meaning of life as he created. Miners tended to be coarse and unattractive in appearance, but are kind and earnest at heart. Their line of work is regarded as lowly by society, but Hung Jui-Lin believed they bore the cross that benefitted the general public. Their contributions and sacrifices shone with humanist glory. Miners were unpolished and were often treated with disregard. They lived a life of acquiescence and lacked confidence, like this miner nicknamed “Ah Dai” (Dummy). Scrawny, alone, and simple-minded, he nevertheless becomes a protagonist in Hung Jui-Lin’s work. He ran errands outside the mines, and was responsible for delivering coal to buyers as well as for assisting in cleaning the work environment. In this work, he is depicted without a headlamp on his hardhat, and does not have a towel draped on his neck. He sits barefooted on the ground and hugs his knees, awaiting instruction. Hung Jui-Lin made this quick pencil sketch of a waiting Ah Dai using intentional blank spaces (liubai) and varying densities of hatching to capture his likeness. Ah Dai seems unaware of and unconcerned with Hung Jui-Lin’s depiction of his expression. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

title: Safety Warning before Entering the Mine

listRow.content: To ensure the safety of the miners, the inspection team reiterate warnings and reminders to miners before the enter the pit at dawn. In this group portrait, eight figures gathered prior to entering the pit. Seven miners surround the one miner facing the artist, forming a space with a foreground and background relationship. The moods of the miners with their faces in profile or turned away from the viewer cannot be discerned. The figure at the center steals a glance, with his eyes wide and a stunned expression as his eyes meet those of the artist. Aside from the unsettled expression of the figure at the center, there is no interaction between the miners who have gathered around him; perhaps they are simply waiting. The sepia tones, ink tones, and a touch of bluish gray set the mood for the entire scene. A light from the lower right creates a clear contrast of light and dark on the miners clothing and produces a solemn atmosphere. The brushwork on this character sketch is free and unfettered, with a consistent line thickness, and crisp turns of the brush. Concerned for his colleague in the mines, Hung Jui-Lin has documented this brief moment before sunrise with his quick brushwork, capturing the miners’ anxious state of mind.       (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

listRow.content: Prior to his group portrait scenarios, Hung Jui-Lin’s creative theme focusing on miners began in the 1950s with portraits of individual miners. Hung oversaw up two hundred miners, and was with them from dawn to dusk. He was able to identify them based solely on their speaking voice and walking posture, without seeing their faces; and was attuned to their personalities and life experiences. The miner in this portrait is Mu Huo, a foreman and right-hand-man under Hung’s father-in-law, Peng Ching. Mu Huo led a team of workers whose jobs involved a high degree of difficulty, and hence was paid a higher wage. He was mindful of saving money so that he could turn his life around, and was an exemplar of a successful minder. The most important condition for a foreman is to provide a stable and skilled labor force. Mu Huo was charismatic with a wide network. His son and son-in-law were both on his team. In Hung Jui-Lin’s drawing, Mu Huo appears to be of a certain age. He is unshaven, with slightly drooping eyelids and jowls. His tranquil demeanor is vividly portrayed. Shaded areas are expressed using pencil hatches. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

title: Portrait of Eldest Son, Chin Shung

listRow.content: This work was created in 1945 in a post-war environment when material resources were in short supply, and access to painting materials was near impossible. Motivated by fatherly love, Hung Jui-Lin painted two portraits of his firstborn son under these arduous conditions: one in pastel, and the other in oil. In this work Chin S. Houng is dressed in his kindergarten pinafore as he sits to pose for his father. Prior to their marriage, Hung Jui-Lin’s wife Peng Jin-Hua worked as a kindergarten teacher in the mining community, so it was expected that Chin S. Houng should attend kindergarten, though few children in the mining community had this opportunity. Hung Jui-Lin captures the child’s innocent visage with assertive brushstrokes. The bright eyes that gaze intently at his father are especially captivating. The illuminated areas of his forehead, left cheek, chin, and left shoulder, stand in contrast to his raven-haired crewcut and the shadows over his right shoulder – creating a natural three-dimensionality to the human figure. Chin S. Houng’s clothing and pinafore are tilted toward the right of the canvas. He was a mischievous child of his clothes. For seven decades, this portrait accompanied Chin S. Houng, hanging on a wall in his bedroom at his residence. He responded to a presumptuous request, and graciously parted with the work so that it can at last be repatriated and presented before the citizenry. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

title: Portrait of Hung Chin Shung at 5 Years Old

listRow.content: Hung Jui-Lin painted this pastel portrait of his first-born son Chin S. Houng, then five years old, in 1945. World War Two had just ended, and Hung Jui-Lin was in a mood of stability that enabled to capture this portrait of his son. By the age of 33, Hung Jui-Lin had become more adept at depicting human figures. This work does not depict the entire head according to traditional methods of composition, but depicts the face, and chest, and a portion of the hair. The character’s facial features captivate the viewer. There was a shortage of material resources in the aftermath of war, and inadequate papers and brushes for painting. In this work, Chun-Hsiung is dressed in white, with illuminated areas painted in pale yellow. The contours of his left cheek, chin, lips, and ears are outlined in reddish brown. These contour lines also become the darkest areas of shading on his face. Though the child’s face is shrouded in shadow, Chun-Hsiung’s cherubic eyes quietly gaze at his father wielding his brush, allowing his father to paint him. The work conveys the tacit understanding and emotional exchange between father and son. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

listRow.content:
This sketch was made in December 1937 in Japan’s Yamagata Prefecture. In the foreground, two local residents wearing large quilts and snow boots stand facing each other in conversation. To their right, children prepare to embark on sleds. There are four figures to their left, wrapped up in overcoats and seemingly also engaged in conversation. In the distance are snow-covered mountains and homes. The sky is overcast and misty, suggesting the severe cold. The scene conveys the local color of a snowy countryside.

The artist’s brushwork is carefree and flowing. He competes this wintry scene in a snowy country within a short time. The variations in the figures’ clothing is exemplary of Hung Jui-Lin’s keen sense of observation. He not only expresses the unique characteristics of the clothing and accessories of each individual, but also vividly conveys their interactive relationship. Hung Jui-Lin’s figures always express a dynamism. His use of rendered diluted colors to fill in and of texturization with rubbed ink to create unified tones with a sense of volume, portend his methodology in sketching miners upon his return to Taiwan. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Snowy Landscape in Yamagata Prefecture

listRow.content:
This work depicts a scene from outside the gates of the Hosoume family home. The roof of the Japanese style dwelling is covered in a thick layer of snow. Walls of snow flank the roadside. A sled is parked outside the front doors of the residence, and a child stands nearby, dressed in snow boots and a hooded coat. Using the simplest of drawing tools, Hung Jui-Lin has depicted an ordinary day in a snowy land that may have been overlooked in the past. The simple drawing, composed as though seen out of a window, gives an impression of a documentary photograph. The authentically conveyed winter atmosphere in the frigid north country vividly captures characteristics of the local culture.

The snow scenes of Yamagata left a profound visual and cultural impression on Hung Jui-Lin. Decades later, he reminisced: “What moved me the most during my years of study in Japan was not the cherry blossoms, or the crystal-clear streams, but the laborers in the frigid weather.” While visiting Japan’s Yamagata Prefecture, Hung Jui-Lin was deeply moved by the farmers’ determination to survive in the frigid landscape, which inspired his sense of concern and respect for laborers. When he returned to Taiwan in 1938 and began working at the Reifang Coalmine, he witnessed the daily struggles of the humble miners to survive. He had a deep sense of care for his hard-working brothers in the mines. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Yamagata Prefecture in Winter

listRow.content: After graduating from the five-year program at Japan’s Imperial Art School (Bijutsu Gakkō) in 1936, Hung Jui-Lin visited his classmate Hosoume Kyuya in Esuoka (Imurayama City), Yamagata Prefecture in December 1937, and stayed with him for a month. While in Esuoka, he witnessed the difficult life of farmers in the harshness of winter and felt a deep sense of compassion for them. During his time with the Hosoume family, he documented scenes of life in the snow-covered land in four large sketch books, showcasing the perseverance and determination of laborers in their struggles against the environment. In this work, he depicts the weight of the snow-covered houses and the textures of timber houses using the monochromatic lines of a pencil. The vast expanse of snow is depicted by the silvery white world. The lightly rendered dark skies offset the whiteness of the snowdrifts. The tactile sense of pencil markings smudged with fingers conveys the moisture in the atmosphere after a snowfall. There is a faint yellow in the work that expresses the weak illumination of the sun through the atmosphere. The child and small dog at the center of the painting are undaunted by the cold and inject a life force into this season unfavorable for crops (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

title: Painting Studio at Teikoku Art School in Japan

listRow.content: This work depicting the art studio at the Tokyo Imperial Art School (Tōkyō Bijutsu Gakkō) in Japan was completed during Hung Jui-Lin’s time as a student at the Department of Western Painting. Although Hung Jui-Lin focused on Western painting, his teacher Shimizu Takashi was both a sculptor and an oil painter, prompting a number of the students at the Department Western Painting to also study sculpture. Sugimoto Kotaro was among the students with an interest in sculpture. He once sculpted a bust of Hung Jui-Lin, which Hung Jui-Lin kept until 1992, when he cast the plaster original into bronze. Engrossed in creating a white sculpture of a hunched figure, the man in the foreground of this painting was presumably Hung’s classmate Kotaro A cushioned rattan chair is pictured in the lower left corner with a human statue on the right, and a bust resting on a wooden rack. Hung Jui-Lin placed great importance on the depiction of light. In the foreground is a backlit scene where human figures and the ground appeared dark, but light spills onto the sculpture and illuminates the floor. Darkness and light demarcate the space in this corner of the studio. The ordinariness of the subject matter conveys the presence of art in the realities of his life. This work is a portrayal of Hung Jui-Lin’s daily life during his studies in Japan. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
