listRow.content: From his school days in the 1930s, to 1964 when he began teaching at the National Taiwan Academy of Arts (now the National Taiwan University of Arts), there was a lapse of 30 years in Hung Jui-Lin’s works on the theme of the female nude. While teaching a class on sketching human figures, he had opportunities to sketch nude models alongside his students. After continuously creating throughout the 1970s and 1980s, he had achieved a state of consummate perfection in his later years. This model in a standing pose faces the viewer in slight profile, with her right hand behind her neck and left arm naturally resting on her side. Her head tilts toward the left, her feet slightly apart. This work was completed in 1935 when he was in his fifth year at the Tokyo Imperial Art School (Tōkyō Bijutsu Gakkō). A pencil was used to outline the silhouette and for shading, after which diluted colors were applied to express the softness of feminine skin. The woman’s hair is also expressed using lines, and her facial features are distinct. Hung Jui-Lin’s calm, unhurried pencil lines can be seen in this work. In addition to the skilled depiction of the female human form, the shading of the diluted color also perfectly showcases the voluptuous undulating form. After five years of painting study, Hung Jui-Lin’s mastery of form appears confident. Though this is merely a sketch of a female nude, it demonstrates the fruits of his rigorous academic training. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

Hung Jui-Lin was admitted to the Western Painting Department at the Imperial Art School (Bijutsu Gakkō) in 1931, so it is likely that this work was completed in his second year of college. Pencil sketches of female nudes are compulsory in the coursework of every painting department. The drawing depicts a back view of the female nude. The model’s left hand rests on her hip, her left foot in front of her right, shifting her weight onto her left, so her hips are uneven. This angle of a female nude from the back, is a necessary lesson in life drawing. Although the pencil cannot express the gradients that charcoal can, Hung Jui-Lin is still able to create light and shadows through lines, and to express the undulating musculature of the back, buttocks, and thigh muscles. A sense of volume is conveyed through the outline of the silhouette, showcasing Hung Jui-Lin’s consideration for the curvatures in the limbs. This work is significantly smaller in dimensions than his practice paintings for the Kawabata Painting School before he was admitted to college. It is likely this was a work completed as daily study. listRow.content: Sketching the female nude has a long tradition in the West. Traditional poses for the models are related to long established aesthetic perspectives. The subject of Hung Jui-Lin sketches are all Eastern women whose proportions are naturally different from that of Westerners. He once offered his observations on the Eastern female physique: “People from the East are different from those from the West. Due to the way of life, nutrition, and other factors. The standard Westerners body follows a 1 to 8 head-to-body ratio. Our bone structures differ due of our environment, we in the East have shorter legs and a longer torso. It is a different body shape.” In his youth, Hung had an accurate grasp on the model’s posture and shifts in focus. The left hand of this model has been hidden from view, but her left shoulder, barely seen, is still depicted along with her left palm positioned behind the hip. She stands feet together in a closed contrapposto pose. The ambiguous spaces in the foreground and background are expressed through light and shade. This work has been marked “12.17,” indicating the date it was created. The femininity and voluptuousness of the Eastern female body is expressed through the proportioned correspondence of various body parts of the female nude. The viewer senses the passion and devotion of this young artist during his time at the Imperial Art School (Bijutsu Gakkō). (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Leaning Female Nude

listRow.content: This work depicting a female nude has the notation of “6.1.1.6” on the lower right. “6.1.” indicates a date, but it is unknown what the “1.6” is a reference to. Charcoal pencil is the most often used tool in classical techniques for sketching the female nude. Compared to the black of graphite pencils, charcoal pencils can achieve a broader range of tones and express richer levels of blacks and whites. Mastering the expression of textures and volumes of the human body in monochrome is the foundation of building skills in Western painting. In his later years, Hung Jui-Lin remarked, “Regardless of the subject of a painting: be it a still life, portrait, or landscape, one must first observe the structure, shape, and lighting of the subject, and then make a plan on how to capture it.” This female nude takes a standing pose, with her body slightly turned in profile; the outside of the left contour line has been reinforced in black to indicate a shadow, and creates a space between the figure and the background. The model’s left arm is raised and flexed, with her hand on her shoulder. Her left-hand rests on her hips as she takes a contrapposto stance with her right leg relaxed. The sense of volume that extends from the left hip to the thigh bring focus to the contours of the body and the areas of illumination. Unlike sketches of plaster works, sketches of human models emphasizes the posture and proportions of the figure, and must convey the supple texture of the flesh body. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Standing Female Nude

listRow.content:
While at the Hongo Painting Institute and then at the Kawabata Painting School during the beginning of his time in Japan, Hung Jui-Lin often practiced using plaster busts as subject. Teachers inspected these exercises, but more often the students were left to their own devices. The early generation of Taiwanese painters who applied to art institutions in Japan went through similarly rigorous practices in sketching to gain admittance. 

Upon entering the Imperial Art School (Bijutsu Gakkō), Hung further delved into the skeletal structure of human bodies and the expressions of lights and shadows on the human body. Recalling this journey, Hung Jui-Lin said “We were Taiwanese, so we had to work much harder than the Japanese.” The model in the drawing is reposed and in profile, with her arm on the back of the chair. Hung Jui-Lin has captured the relaxed pose and pensive demeanor. The model’s center of gravity is on her hip, with her right calf slightly flexed; the retracted space and supportive force is more difficult to depict, but he manages to grasp it. This sketch of a female nude preserved from this period is a testament to Hung Jui-Lin’s foundation in the human anatomy and his tireless attitude toward learning. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Seated Female Nude

title: Plaster Bust, Marcus Junius Brutus Caepio

listRow.content: This practice sketch was signed “A Hung Jui-Lin” on the upper right corner. The letter “A” here may either designate a class session or grade marked by an instructor without additional points of reference. Another “A” has been marked on the lower left corner. This type of work reveals Hung Jui-Lin’s foundation in sketching before he enrolled at the art institute, and indicates the level of sketching proficiency prerequisite at Japanese art institutions at the time. The plaster bust is of Marcus Junius Brutus Caepio (85-42 BC), the founder of the Roman Republic, renowned for his dedication to the Roman Republic and to freedom. His mother was mistress to Julius Caesar. Brutus later participated in the assassination of Caesar, and gave rise to the Shakespearian quote “not that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved Rome more.” This bust of a young man with patrician features is a subject often depicted by beginner painters. It has has been illuminated from the right, casting its left profile in shadow. Two-thirds of the face are in gradients of darkness, while the illuminated side of the face are in degrees of brightness. The profile is emphasized with thick black lines, producing three-dimensionality on a two-dimensional plane, and showcasing Hung Jui-Lin’s adroit sketching techniques. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Plaster Bust, Marcus Junius Brutus Caepio

listRow.content: This sketch was made by Hung Jui-Lin at the age of 18 as he made preparations to take the entrance exam for art school. The work is signed on the top right corner with “October 10, before noon Hung,” indicating that the work was completed in the morning of October 10, 1930. The work is similar to Plaster Bust, Lucius Junius Brutus-1 in that it also depicts a plaster bust from an upward angle, but the work varies in the angle of the profile. This sketch of Brutus in profile is on point in terms of form, light, texture, and the depiction of folds in the crepe robe. For a plaster bust, a variation in the light source is reflected in the changes in the shadows. Using charcoal pencil to express the plaster textures and the subtle variations in shadows and light requires detailed observation and careful contemplation. Carved by Michelangelo in 1537-1538 A.D., the original Brutus bust is a marble sculpture measuring 74 centimeters in height. and currently in the collection of the Bargello Palace National Museum in Florence. If Michelangelo’s David and Moses are the embodiment of idealized heroes, then this Bust of Brutus is a hero with an existence in reality with agency and an internal spiritual power. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
listRow.Title: Plaster Bust, Lucius Junius Brutus-2

listRow.content: Accompanied by Chen Chih-Chi, Hung Jui-Lin arrived in Tokyo in September 1930 with plans to sit the art academy admissions exam the following spring. In making preparations, Hung Jui-Lin spent his days at the Western Painting Department of the Kawabata Painting School, where he focused on improving his sketching abilities using plaster busts as subject. He once said the classical academic sketching style taught these two institutions was better suited to his personality. The numbers “12 20” written on the upper right corner of this practice sketch of a plaster bust presumably refers to the date December 20, 1930. The bust is of Lucius Junius Brutus, founder of the Roman Republic and traditionally considered to be the first consul of Rome. He was a man of honor and integrity, and a heroic figure who protected democracy above personal interests. This work takes an upward angle; a similar sketch of the plaster bust from a different angle is dated October 10, indicating that Hung Jui-Lin practiced sketching the bust from a variety of angles. This work uses charcoal to express the textures, illumination, and shadows on the white plaster bust. There are areas of brightness even in the shadows, with a richness of tones in between, and a plethora of details that fully express the dimensionality of the bust. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

title: Plum Blossom, Orchid, Bamboo and Chrysanthemum (4 pieces)

listRow.Title: Plum Blossom, Orchid, Bamboo and Chrysanthemum (4 pieces)

listRow.content: At the age of eight in 1920, Hung Jui-Lin entered the Daojiang Private Charity School (Daojiang Gijuku) on Liuguan Street in Dadaocheng, where his teacher Wu Ching-Hai discovered his unique artistic talent. Wu purchased Japanese art magazines and catalogs with his own funds so Hung Jui-Lin could begin by emulating the works of the masters. This encounter with Western art was a watershed moment for Hung Jui-Lin. This work, Michelangelo Study, was completed when Hung was 12 years old. The work is signed and dated “1924 6 9 An Sui Rin,” which was the Hokkien pronunciation of Hung Jui-Lin’s name. A note on the back indicates, “模寫ミクラレチェロ” (A Study of Michelangelo). Sketches preserved from the same period emulate works by Jean-François Millet and other Western artists, including still lifes, portraits, and landscapes. This particular work can be regarded as the launching point of Hung Jui-Lin’s journey into Western painting. Emulating the works of the masters gave him an understanding of the degree of completion and standards in a sketch work. The turbulent brushstrokes on the canvas, the overlapping curved lines that reveal darkness and light, and the depiction of human forms are remarkably precise, revealing Hung Jui-Lin’s extraordinary talent for painting. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)

title: Waiting Miners
medium: Ink and pigment on cotton paper

listRow.content: Miners work in team units. The members on a team support each other through happiness and hardship. They must get along and be able to help one another. Their salaries are calculated as a group and then equally divided. A senior member in each team is the team leader or foreman. He must be able to manage any situation that arises, and to lead the team to resolve any issues. Every task in the pit requires mutual cooperation to see to fruition. The miners develop a tacit understanding after working together for a time, and the team members forge deep mutual connections. They would invite each other for drinks after work, and resolve any conflicts over drinks. This painting depicts six miners. Whether they form a team cannot be confirmed, however, Huang Jui-Lin hopes to express the daily routines of the miners through such group portrait. The two men on the left, with their backs toward the viewer, seem to be deep in conversation. Shirtless and in long trousers, the man on the left stands with his arm akimbo, looking straight ahead, vividly conjuring the conditions when miners come together. Intersecting shadows on the ground are depicted with a few strokes of diluted ink. There is a harmony to the expression of light and shadows and the tones of the clothing on the figures. Whether on the rise, the pivot, or in his straight lines, Hung Jui-Lin adroitly wields his brush with a steadfast confidence. (Pai Hsueh-Lan).

title: Taking a Break in the Mine

listRow.content:
The interior of a mine pit is unbearably warm at over 36 degrees Celsius. Scattering dust and falling rocks are a constant. Miners perspire profusely even when they are not moving, and sometimes are so warm that they strip down to their underpants, like the miner dressed in thong underwear in this painting. According to regulation, mine drifts are supported by props and bars made of acacia wood, with the distance between props not to exceed one meter apart. The two miners portrayed in this work are seated within a narrow space framed by a wooden bar and two props, perhaps taking a break during a lull, while Hung Jui-Lin used the break to make sketches. 

A stretch of mine drift lies beyond behind the figure. Miners must maintain a specific posture over extended periods when mining, which can be quite arduous. Hung Jui-Lin has captured the expression of submission on the miner’s face. This is a momentary respite that does not allow for complete relaxation. The body must be ready to continue its toil. As Hung Jui-Lin said, they are angels bearing crosses. The work appears to have been trimmed, and the image is incomplete, with only half of the figure on the left shown. (Pai Hsueh-Lan)
